paragraphs.text: 14.1. Definitions
paragraphs.heading: Part 14. Appeals

sentences.text: Definitions

paragraphs.text: (1) In this Part, (a) “appeal” means an appeal to the Court of Appeal governed by this Part; (b) “appellant” means a person who under an enactment or these rules (i) files an application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal, or (ii) files a notice of appeal; (c) “case management officer” means a person appointed as a case management officer under the Court of Appeal Act; (d) “Civil Appeal Hearing List” means the list referred to in rule 14.33(1) that identifies selected appeals that have been scheduled for oral argument and the date on which each oral argument is to be heard; (e) “court appealed from” means the court, person or tribunal from which an appeal has been brought; (e.1) “Court of Appeal Management System” means the system established by the Court of Appeal for purposes including creating, issuing, filing, accessing, transmitting, storing, recording, providing or submitting documents or information by electronic means in respect of matters under this Part; (f) “decision” means the whole or any part of the decision of the court, person or tribunal from which an appeal lies and includes a judgment, order, decision, verdict, direction, determination or award and, where the context requires, includes the verdict or finding of a jury; (g) “fast track appeal” means an appeal that must be managed in accordance with rule 14.14; (h) “file” means to submit the correct document through the Court of Appeal Management System or otherwise as permitted in accordance with the Court of Appeal of Alberta Practice Direction — Electronic Filing, adopted by the Alberta Court of Appeal and as amended from time to time, and obtain an acknowledgment by the Registrar that the document has been accepted for filing; (i) “judge”, when used in reference to the Court of Appeal, includes the Chief Justice of Alberta, the justices of appeal and the supernumerary judges of the Court of Appeal; (j) “panel” means three or more judges of the Court of Appeal unless the Chief Justice, in case of emergency, declares that two judges may form a panel; (k) “party” means a party to an appeal or an application under this Part and includes an intervenor where the context requires; (l) “Registrar” means a person appointed as a Registrar of the Court of Appeal under the Court of Appeal Act and includes a Deputy Registrar of the Court of Appeal and any person designated by a Registrar or the Chief Justice of Alberta to act for a Registrar; (m) “respondent” means, unless the context otherwise requires, the person who, under an enactment or these rules, (i) is named as a respondent to an application for permission to appeal, or (ii) is named as a respondent to an appeal; (n) “standard appeal” means an appeal other than a fast track appeal. (o) [Repealed Alta. Reg. 61/2023, s. 3(c).] (2) Where a respondent files a notice of cross appeal, unless this Part otherwise provides, the rules relating to appeals apply to the cross appeal and, in particular, (a) references to an appeal include a cross appeal; (b) references to an appellant include a respondent who files a notice of cross appeal; (c) references to a respondent include an appellant who is named as a respondent in a notice of cross appeal; (d) references to parties to an appeal include parties to a cross appeal. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4; 61/2023, s. 3

sentences.text: Application of general rules

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to this Part, to any enactment, and to any direction by an appeal judge, if this Part does not deal with a matter, other Parts of these rules apply to appeals, with any appropriate modifications. (2) Where a rule in this Part provides that a specific rule in another Part applies to appeals, the specific rule applies with any appropriate modifications. (3) Rule 13.5(1) does not apply to a time period or deadline referred to in this Part. (4) Subject to any appropriate modifications or any direction by an appeal judge, when applying the provisions of any other Part to an appeal under this Part, (a) a reference to the court clerk or a court officer is to be read as a reference to the Registrar; (b) a reference to a plaintiff is to be read as a reference to an appellant; (c) a reference to a defendant is to be read as a reference to a respondent; (d) a reference to the court or a judge are to be read as a reference to an appeal judge; (e) a reference to a pleading or commencement document includes a reference to a notice of appeal, a notice of cross appeal or an application for permission to appeal. (5) In this Part, “appropriate modifications” means those changes and modifications to the use and interpretation of these rules necessary or appropriate for a rule in another Part to apply to and to be used in appellate practice. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4

sentences.text: Right to appeal

paragraphs.text: (1) Except as otherwise provided, an appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from the whole or any part of a decision of a Court of King's Bench judge sitting in court or chambers, or the verdict or finding of a jury. (2) No appeal is allowed to the Court of Appeal from the dismissal by a Court of King's Bench judge of an application made without notice. (3) Where an application has been made to the Court of King's Bench without notice and has been dismissed, the applicant may reapply (a) on notice, if the dismissal was for lack of notice, or (b) by renewal of the application if the dismissal was for reasons other than the lack of notice. (4) No appeal is allowed directly to the Court of Appeal from a decision of an applications judge. (5) No appeal is allowed (a) from a judgment granting a divorce, on or after the date on which the divorce takes effect, or (b) unless an appeal judge extends the time, from an order made in a divorce proceeding, more than 30 days after the date on which the order was made. Alta. Reg. 41/2014, s. 4; 136/2022, s. 1(11); 218/2022, s. 10(6)

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.4:1 Rule 14.4 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.4. 1. Right to Appeal is Statutory In Québec (Communauté urbaine) v. Services de santé du Québec, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 426, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that the right to appeal is a right created by statute. At pp. 431–32 and 435, Madam Justice L'Heureux-Dubé, speaking for the court, said: The majority of the Court of Appeal rejected this argument as well, as in its opinion: … The right of appeal is a substantive right, an exceptional right which (except for a question of excess of jurisdiction by the Supreme Court, which is not the case here, Goodman v. Rompkey et al., [1982] 1 S.C.R. 589), exists only if specifically created by legislation and only to the extent provided therein (Welch v. R., [1950] S.C.R. 412 at 428) … … as the majority of the Court of Appeal pointed out, the right of appeal is a statutory creation, the very existence of which is subject to precise rules … 2. Appealing Interim Orders In Anand v. Anand, 2016 ABCA 23, the Court had before it an appeal of an interim spousal support order made by Queen's Bench justice sitting in Chambers. The Court made these comments about appeals of interim orders: 66 Interim spousal support orders have inherent frailties; the evidentiary record is inevitably incomplete. Here, the viva voce special chambers judge had no ability to consider the interplay between spousal support and the division of matrimonial property, which future division may allow the respondent to generate income from assets. 67 This Court has repeatedly urged that parties not waste finite time and money appealing interim orders—time and money better spent achieving an equitable settlement, or getting a final determination at trial of all matters in issue: Hartley v Del Pero, 2010 ABCA 182 at para 27, 487 AR 248; Zaboschuk v Zaboschuk, 2012 ABCA 172 at para 5, [2012] A.J. No. 575 (QL); Davies v Davies, 2015 ABCA 17 at para 6, [2015] A.J. No. 35 (QL); FJN at para 6. 3. Moot Appeals An appeal is moot whether or not it suggests general questions of law or jurisdiction which could affect nonparties. Given the laws of precedent, most appeals suggest such questions. There are some exceptions to the general rule against deciding moot appeals. … Indeed, there are so many recent reported cases in Canada applying those exceptions, that one might gain the impression that the exception is the rule, and that appeals will rarely be dismissed as moot. That is not the law. There are real dangers in hearing moot appeals, quite apart from the obvious waste of court resources. One danger is that a proceeding could go more or less by default, even by collusion, because a respondent would have little motive to fight it. That is not likely here. But sometimes the respondent may have a view or interest somewhat different from many or most people, leading him to be unaware of certain arguments. Once the substantive issue has been settled, counsel may not recognize relevant authorities as relevant. … Another danger is that relevant arguments will not be put before the appeal court. That could occur for the same reason. But there are other reasons that the arguments might be incomplete. One is that there can be no remedies in a moot suit, so issues must be split and only abstract ones be decided. Another reason is that counsel thinking in the abstract without a specific factual problem will not imagine practical difficulties. … An abstract discussion of the law is likely to produce a vague judgment, difficult to apply in practice with any certainty. Some government References to Canadian appellate courts in the past have illustrated that. Anyone who asks a vague question is likely to get a vague answer. A third danger is that the court may be led to enunciate a rule of law which hangs together in theory or logic, but is simply impractical. Law exists for living human beings, but groups of human beings do not always act logically and consistently. Sometimes it takes an actual dispute, or several, and experience, to show what will work and what will not. A fourth danger is that the court hearing a moot appeal will enunciate too wide a rule of law. Sometimes it is better to build the law a piece at a time, by trial and error, proceeding from one specific dispute to another. Sometimes one must do that, because the topic is otherwise too complex, difficult, or unforeseeable. A fifth danger is that the court will proceed with an inadequate evidentiary record. That is particularly apposite here, where the appeal books seem to contain no evidence at all, except maybe a short report by an investigating officer employed by the Board. If the union local led any evidence before the Board, it was not transcribed. No one filed any affidavit in Queen's Bench. Even if any facts were asserted to the Board in any of the written arguments, they have not been sworn to, nor been open to cross-examination. Sometimes a respondent may have a smaller war chest than the appellant, or less motivation to spend large sums. That too can lead to a lopsided record in a moot suit. A sixth danger is that the moot appeal dragoons the respondent into acting as a sort of private Attorney General, or devil's advocate. He or she must spend time and money on a question in which he or she has no present interests at risk. That is unfair to him or her. It may be useful to the appellant, or even to society, to clarify or build case law. But why should the respondent have to finance that? He or she is not the Legislature, nor even the Law Reform Institute. This may be akin to forcing a litigant to buy law books and donate them to the courthouse library. …Wiebe v. Labour Relations Board (Alta.) (2001), 281 A.R. 362 (C.A.) at 364-365, per curiam. 4. Application to Open Judgment Is Not an Appeal Actually, the application to open up my judgment is not, by its very nature, an appeal; rather it is an invitation to review a decision properly made at the time, but one which seeks variance because of the defendant's contention that the evidence which he provided me at the time (by affidavit) was erroneous. The matter of weighing his former evidence with his fresh evidence would seem to be the exercising of the function of a court of original jurisdiction rather than that of a Court of Appeal. National Arts Services Corp. v. Bank of British Columbia (1981), 16 Alta. L.R. (2d) 111 (Q.B.), at 115, per Cormack J. 5. When Appeal Lies to Court of Appeal … the appeal to this court only lies from an otherwise unimpeachable, unappealable, order of the Court of Queen's Bench. C & A Electric Industries Ltd. v. Gitersos (1983), 43 A.R. 234 at 236 (C.A.). C & A Electric Industries Ltd. was applied in Opi Ltd. v. Harway Industrial Enterprises Ltd. (1986), 47 Alta. L.R. (2d) 142 (C.A.). If the appeal is as of right, no conditions on that right can be imposed. According to Rule 505, because there is no statutory provision or Rule to the contrary, the appellant is entitled to appeal the order to this Court without leave. Since leave is not required, no conditions on the right of appeal could be prescribed by this panel. Horner v. Adams (1996), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 223 (C.A.), at 224, per curiam. 6. Who May Appeal In Marcaronies Hair Club and Laser Center Inc v. Bank of Montreal, 2021 ABCA 40, 2021 CarswellAlta 235, the Court discussed who could bring an appeal pursuant to Rule 14.4: [37] It is correct that Rule 14.4(1) provides for an appeal to this Court from a decision of the Queen's Bench. But notably, the Rule does not say who may appeal. That is to be determined by this Court based on the applicable legislation and the Court's jurisdiction under the Judicature Act. Rule 14.4(1) also includes the caveat “except as otherwise provided”, clearly implying therefore that any such claimed right to appeal under the Rules may be curtailed by other provisions. This is reinforced by Rule 1.9 which provides that an enactment prevails over the Rules to the extent of any inconsistency. … … 41] As noted, this Court has recognized that there may be exceptional circumstances in which it would be appropriate to grant permission to appeal: Brewer; Société des Acadiens v Association of Parents, 1986 CanLII 66 (SCC), [1986] 1 SCR 549 at 594 [Société des Acadiens]. The Legislature has conferred broad authority on this Court under s 3 of the Judicature Act to entertain appeals from any decision of the Court of Queen's Bench. … [42] The test for whether a non-party should be granted permission to appeal centers on whether they would have been a proper party to the action. That involves considering a number of factors, including whether their interests were represented at the proceeding: Société des Acadiens at 594. … 7. Only Formal Judgment Can Be Appealed In Elizabeth Metis Settlement v. Metis Settlements General Council (2004), 346 A.R. 86 (C.A.), orders were granted by a Chambers judge. The decisions set out in the orders were not appealed, but the appellant did take issue with comments made by the learned Chambers judge in her reasons for decision. The Court of Appeal held that one could not appeal the reasons in the absence of an appeal of the decision. At p. 87, Berger J.A. said: … The Appellant acknowledges that it takes issue only with certain comments made by the presiding justice in chambers in her reasons for decision. We do not view the impugned comments of the trial judge as declaratory in nature. Only the formal disposition of a court can properly be the subject of appellate review. The reasons, in a given case, may arguably taint the resulting order, in which case if the order is appealed, appellate intervention may be warranted. But where no appeal is taken from the order pronounced in the court below, the appellate court is without jurisdiction to intervene. … In Kennedy v. Trustees for the 1985 Sawridge Trust, 2017 ABCA 439, 2017 CarswellAlta 2698, the Court said: 8 Rule 14.8(1), which measures the time in which an appeal must be filed from the date of “pronouncement”, does not expand the scope of a permissible appeal to cover everything “pronounced” in the reasons for decision. Appeals are only available from a “judgment, order or decision”, not the reasons. Comments by the trial judge that do not form a part of his adjudication, and accordingly do not find their way into the formal order, cannot support an appeal. In CCS Corporation v. Secure Energy Service, 2018 ABCA 120, 2018 CarswellAlta 573, 68 Alta. L.R. (6th) 274, 80 B.L.R. (5th) 228, 17 C.P.C. (8th) 284, [2018] 6 W.W.R. 575, “the appellant sought an order or declaration that certain findings of fact made by the case management judge do not apply to the Secure Respondents.” The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal “on jurisdictional grounds” and said: 13 We conclude this court has no jurisdiction to hear the appeal on the merits. 14 An appeal is from a decision, not from the reasons: Rayani v Yule & Company (Hong Kong) Limited, 1996 ABCA 35 at para 13; Elizabeth Metis Settlement v Metis Settlement General Council, 2004 ABCA 39 at para 1; SemCanada Crude Company (Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act), 2009 ABCA 244 at para 7; R v Elliott, 2014 ABCA 431 at para 4; and Huartt v Specialized Property Evaluation Control Services Ltd, 2016 ABCA 142 at para 6. 15 As noted by this court in Elizabeth Metis Settlement at para 1, “Only the formal disposition of a court can properly be the subject of appellate review”. 16 Further, r 14.4(1) of the Rules of Court provides that: Except as otherwise provided, an appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from the whole or any part of a decision of a Court of Queen's Bench judge sitting in court or chambers, or the verdict or finding of a jury. 17 Rule 14.1(1)(f) goes on to define “decision” as “the whole or any part of the decision of the court, person or tribunal from which an appeal lies and includes a judgment, order, decision, verdict, direction, determination or award and, where the context requires, includes the verdict or finding of a jury.” 18 The appellant did not appeal the decision to dismiss all of the claims against Pembina, save one. Rather, the appellant seeks a declaration that certain of the case management judge's findings do not bind it. Such a declaration raises issues of res judicata and issue estoppel that should properly be decided by the trial judge. In ServiceMaster of Canada Limited v. Meyer, 2019 ABCA 130, 2019 CarswellAlta 2118, 92 Alta. L.R. (6th) 222, 93 B.L.R. (5th) 121, 57 C.C.E.L. (4th) 175, [2019] 11 W.W.R. 73, Justice Wakeling said: [31] The Alberta Rules of Court[7] allow a party to appeal against features of an order or judgment. In the absence of a statutory provision to the contrary, which does not exist here, a party cannot appeal against reasons. This statement was quoted with approval in Kaufmann v. Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2019 ABCA 272, 2019 CarswellAlta 1375 at paragraph 9. In Castle Building Centres Group Ltd. v. Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply Inc., 2023 ABCA 298, the Court of Appeal, at paragraph 12, reiterated that “[a]n appeal is from the order granted, not the reasons for it.” 8. Scope of Appellate Review The Court of Appeal for Alberta enjoys a broad jurisdiction. The Judicature Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. J-1, s. 3, states: 3. The Court of Appeal (a) has all the jurisdiction and powers possessed by the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories en banc immediately before the Court's organization, and (b) has jurisdiction and power, subject to the Rules of Court, to hear and determine (i) all applications for new trials, (ii) all questions or issues of law, (iii) all questions or points in civil or criminal cases, (iv) all appeals or motions in the nature of appeals respecting a judgment, order or decision of (A) a judge of the Court of Queen's Bench, or (B) a judge of a court of inferior jurisdiction when an appeal is given by any other Act. The provisions of the Judicature Act are supplemented by the Alberta Rules of Court, in particular rules 505 and 518 … These broad powers must, however, be read in light of the principles guiding appellate review as laid down by this court. In particular it has been said on a number of occasions that where a trial judge makes a finding of fact based on the credibility of witnesses, an appeal court should not overturn that finding unless it can be shown that the finding was “palpably wrong”… The Alberta Court of Appeal has itself applied this restriction on a number of occasions. In Colberg v. Schumacher (1978), 12 A.R. 183 … Moir J.A. said at p. 190: In my respectful opinion the learned trial judge could have found that there was an acceptance of the appellant's offer by the respondent. He did not do so. Rather, he chose to accept the evidence given by the respondent in chief. He heard the witness. It was for the trial judge to decide if he accepted the whole of the respondent's evidence, part of it, or none of it. Clearly he accepted the respondent's evidence in chief only. The question is are we entitled to reverse that finding when there is evidence to support that finding? As I read the authorities, particularly the Supreme Court of Canada in Stein v. The Ship “Kathy K”, [1976] 2 S.C.R. 802, we can only do so if the learned trial judge was ‘palpably wrong’. I do not think that he was, particularly in the light of the whole of the cross examination. The learned trial judge had an advantage that we can never have. He saw and heard the respondent give the evidence. I am not prepared to say that he lost the advantage by making the finding he made. Similar cautionary comments may be found in Carter v. Ferguson, [1943] 2 W.W.R. 38 (Alta. C.A.); Clarke v. Gerbrandt (1984), 34 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 (C.A.), and Angus v. Edmonton (1977), 3 A.R. 116 (C.A.). In the last two decisions the Court of Appeal did overturn the findings of a trial judge, but in Clarke on the ground that there was no evidence at all to support the finding and in Angus on the ground that the finding was based on expert evidence where credibility was not a factor. Such circumstances constitute exceptions to the general rule requiring palpable and overriding error. Molchan v. Omega Oil & Gas Ltd. (1988), 57 Alta. L.R. (2d) 193 at 217–18 (S.C.C.). Although the above quote comes from the dissenting reasons of Wilson J., it can be taken as a correct statement of the law relating to the scope of appellate review. 9. Standards of Review In Al-Ghamdi v. College and Association of Registered Nurses of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 81, 2020 CarswellAlta 369, 71 Admin. L.R. (6th) 223, 1 C.C.L.I. (6th) 40, the Court of Appeal set out the standards of review for a number of types of appeals: [6] The standard of review on questions of law is correctness, on questions of fact is palpable and overriding error, and on questions of mixed law and fact is palpable and overriding error unless there is an extricable error of law: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, paras 7–37, [2002] 2 SCR 235. [7] The standard of review with respect to the finding of civil contempt varies with the issue. Where the appeal involves a question of law, the standard of review is correctness. Where the issue relates to the exercise of discretion, the standard is one of reasonableness. Findings of fact and inferences of fact underlying a finding of contempt are reviewed for palpable and overriding error. The finding of contempt in a particular case involves the application of a legal standard to the facts, meaning it is a mixed question of fact and law and is reviewable on the palpable and overriding error standard: Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2015 ABCA 29, paras 25-26, 593 AR 368; RO v DF, 2016 ABCA 170, para 29, 36 Alta LR (6th) 282; Lymer v Jonsson, 2018 ABCA 36, paras 18-19, leave denied [2018] SCCA No 193. [8] The standard of review on whether a litigant is vexatious is discretionary and, absent an error of law, is reviewed for reasonableness: Liu v Matrikon Inc., 2010 ABCA 383, paras 10, 16–17, 493 AR 378; Thompson v International Union of Operating Engineers Local No 995, 2017 ABCA 193, para 23, [2017] AJ No 620. [9] The standard of review with respect to the proper interpretation of rr 3.15, 3.28, 3.68 and 7.3 is correctness. With respect to the application of those rules to findings of fact where the chambers judge has exercised discretion, the standard of review is reasonableness: McGowan v Lang, 2015 ABCA 217, para 21, 602 AR 168; O'Connor Associates Environmental Inc v MEC OP LLC, 2014 ABCA 140, para 12, [2014] 6 WWR 231. [10] In striking a claim under r 3.68(2)(d) as disclosing no reasonable claim or for abuse of process the standard of review is correctness: Waquan v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 279, para 16, [2018] 4 WWR 361; Vanmaele v Maryniak, 2018 ABCA 179, para 6, [2018] AJ No 601. However, assessment of the facts, application of the law to the facts, and ultimate determination as to whether to strike a claim, is discretionary and subject to reasonableness: Grenon v Canada Revenue Agency, 2017 ABCA 96, para 4, 49 Alta LR (6th) 228; Nammo v Canada (Justice and Attorney General), 2015 ABCA 389, para 7, 609 AR 189; O'Connor, paras 11 and 13. [11] The standard of review on the exercise of judicial discretion to refuse permission to amend pleadings is reviewable on the standard of reasonableness: AB v CD, 2008 ABCA 51, paras 9-10, 291 DLR (4th) 359; Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated v Canada (Attorney General), 2009 NUCA 2, para 23, 457 AR 320. [12] With respect to the orders for summary judgment, such orders are discretionary and, absent an error of law, are reviewed for reasonableness: 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49, para 7, 593 AR 391; Warkentin v Klein, 2009 ABCA 223, para 6, 457 AR 73; Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147, para 27, 602 AR 62. In Al-Ghamdi v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 71, 2020 CarswellAlta 285, 68 Admin. L.R. (6th) 290, 6 Alta. L.R. (7th) 42, the Court set out the following standards of review: [9] The standards of review on a statutory appeal from an administrative tribunal are the same as those on other appeals: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para. 49. Those standards of review can be summarized as follows: (a) conclusions on issues of law are reviewed for correctness: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33 at para. 8, [2002] 2 SCR 235. That includes questions of statutory interpretation, including interpretation of the tribunal's “home statute”. (b) findings of fact, including inferences drawn from the facts, are reviewed for palpable and overriding error: Housen at paras. 10, 23; H.L. v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 SCC 25 at para. 74, [2005] 1 SCR 401. (c) findings on questions of mixed fact and law call for a “higher standard” of review, because “matters of mixed law and fact fall along a spectrum of particularity”: Housen at paras. 28, 36. A deferential standard is appropriate where the decision results more from a consideration of the evidence as a whole, but a correctness standard can be applied when the error arises from the statement of the legal test: Housen at paras. 33, 36. (d) issues of fairness and natural justice are reviewed, having regard to the context, to see whether the appropriate level of “due process” or “fairness” required by the statute or the common law has been granted: Vavilov at para. 77. (e) the test on review for bias is whether a reasonable person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, and after having obtained the necessary information and thinking things through, would have a reasonable apprehension of bias. In Schneider v. Homenick, 2024 ABCA 344, additional reasons 2025 ABCA 39, the Court said: [14] The standard of review on questions of law is correctness, on questions of fact is palpable and overriding error, and on questions of mixed law and fact is palpable and overriding error unless there is an extricable error of law: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, paras 7-37, [2002] 2 SCR 235; R v Le, 2019 SCC 34, para 23, [2019] 2 SCR 692; R v Ledesma, 2021 ABCA 143, para 32, 403 CCC (3d) 268, leave to appeal to SCC denied, 2022 CanLII 26226. [15] Palpable and overriding error is a highly deferential standard. “Palpable” means that an error is obvious. “Overriding” means an error that goes to the very core of the outcome of a case: Benhaim v St-Germain, 2016 SCC 48, paras 38, 39, [2016] 2 SCR 352; R v Kruk, 2024 SCC 7, paras 97, 98, 433 CCC (3d) 301. 10. Appeals Involving the Rules of Court In Courtoreille v. Edmonton (City), 2008 ABCA 90, 2008 CarswellAlta 273, 429 A.R. 58, the Court discussed the appropriate standard of review. At paragraph 6, the Court said: 6 The standard of review was recently stated in Phillips v. Cowan, [2007] A.J. No. 319, 2007 ABCA 101 at para. 4: The proper interpretation of the Rules of Court is a matter of law and reviewable on a correctness standard. The application of a the rule to a set of facts is a question of mixed fact and law and subject to the standard of palpable and overriding error. … In Golden Estate v. Neilson, 2011 ABCA 338, 2011 CarswellAlta 2281, 519 A.R. 165, 65 Alta. L.R. (5th) 119, 23 C.P.C. (7th) 14, 539 W.A.C. 165, the Court said, at paragraphs 12-13: 12 An interpretation of the Rules of Court is reviewable on a standard of correctness. However, orders relating to the nature and scope of questioning (formerly, examinations for discovery) are within a chambers judge's discretion and are entitled to considerable deference: Tremco Incorporated v Gienow Building Products Ltd, 2000 ABCA 105, 255 AR 273 and Devon Canada Corporation v PE-Pittsfield LLC, 2008 ABCA 393, 446 AR 62. 13 The standard of review is therefore that found in Trout Lake Store Inc v Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 at para 17, 330 AR 379: The proper interpretation of the Rules is a matter of law which is reviewable on the standard of correctness. The application of the Rules to a set of facts is a matter of mixed fact and law and subject to the standard of palpable and overriding error. 11. Appeals from Discretionary Orders … the standard of review for the exercise of the discretion whether to grant summary judgment, or strike a claim, or to permit a matter to go to trial, is whether an error of law has been made or the decision is unreasonable in that no weight or insufficient weight has been given to relevant considerations. See Russell Food Equipment (Calgary) Ltd. v. Valleyfield Investments Ltd. (1962), 40 W.W.R. (N.S.) 292 (Alta.). Blomme v. Herman (1993), 145 A.R. 16 (C.A.), at 17-18, per the court. In Prefontaine v. Veale (2003), 24 Alta. L.R. (4th) 223 (C.A.), the Court said, at p. 229: Initial appellate review occurs in two stages. First, the appellate court, applying a standard of correctness, considers whether an error of law has been made: Housen v. Nikolaisen, [2002] 2 S.C.R. 235 at 247 (S.C.C.). If no error of law was made, the first appellate court next considers whether the decision arrived at was reasonable. The standard of review at this stage, absent an extricable error in principle, is palpable and overriding error: Housen v. Nikolaisen at p. 248. And Lieberman J.A. said: … this court will not normally interfere with the discretion exercised by a chambers judge but is entitled to do so in certain circumstances. Those circumstances are, to a great extent, outlined by Lord Diplock in Birkett v. James, [1977] 2 All E.R. 801 (H.L.), where that learned law lord said at p. 804: Where leave is granted, an appellate court ought not to substitute its own ‘discretion’ for that of the judge merely because its members would themselves have regarded the balance as tipped against the way in which he had decided the matter. They should regard their function as primarily a reviewing function and should reverse his decision only in cases either (1) where they are satisfied that the judge has erred in principle by giving weight to something which he ought not to have taken into account or by failing to give weight to something which he ought to take into account; Demarco Oil & Gas Inc. v. 309506 Alberta Ltd. (1993), 14 C.P.C. (3d) 71 at 72 (C.A.). 12. Case Management Orders—Standard of Review In Ashraf v. SNC Lavalin ATP Inc., 2017 ABCA 95, 2017 CarswellAlta 462, the Court said: 4 The first two decisions being contested are case management decisions. This Court has made clear that such decisions are entitled to considerable deference. In Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney General), 2015 ABCA 253, 606 AR 291, the Court stated at para 8: Case management judges are owed deference. Absent an error of law, this Court will not interfere with a chambers judge's exercise of discretion unless the result was unreasonable. This is particularly so when many competing factors must be balanced: Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2004 ABCA 279 at para 10 (2004), 354 AR 279. 5 The third decision goes further and deals with the merits of the summary judgment application. The standard of review for the case management judge's conclusions on this subject was described in Dingwall v Dornan, 2014 ABCA 89, 572 AR 106 at para 19: Absent an error of law, the standard of review on an appeal of a summary judgment is reasonableness, given the discretionary nature of the remedy. Questions of law are reviewed for correctness. Errors of mixed fact and law, and errors of fact alone are reviewed on the standard of palpable and overriding error, unless the error of mixed fact and law involves an error relating to an extricable principle of law, in which case the standard is one of correctness: Condominium Corp No 0321365 v 970365 Alberta Ltd, 2012 ABCA 26 at paras 39 and 40, 519 AR 322, see also Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 at para 84. 13. Order Transcript of Chambers Judge's Reasons It is imperative that counsel who are appealing a chambers order obtain a transcript of the chambers judge's reasons. The Court of Appeal has invoked R. 599.1 to award non-recoverable costs against both appellant and respondent when they failed to order the transcript in a timely fashion (see annotation under R. 599.1). In Gunderson v. Jenkins (1998), 216 A.R. 344 (C.A.), the court said, at p. 345: We are all of the view that the appellant should have his costs of this appeal, with the exception of any costs in connection with the appeal book. We are specifically excluding costs connected to the appeal book because, although the reasons of the chambers judge were recorded, they were not transcribed and included in the appeal book. It has taken some considerable effort on our part to obtain them from counsel. The bar cannot continue to ignore the fact that reasons are ususally recorded in chambers in the Court of Queen's Bench, at least in special chambers. They can then be transcribed, and they should be transcribed and included in the appeal book. It is important that we have the reasons of the chambers judge before us when we consider an appeal. 14. Appeal of Liability Trial Before Damage Trial Heard In Jen-Col Construction Ltd. v. Parkland (County) No. 31 (2000), 269 A.R. 352 (Q.B.), an order had previously been granted permitting the severance of liability and damages into two separate trials. The issue then became whether the decision in the liability trial could be appealed before the trial on damages was held. In holding that it could, Veit, J., at p. 354, said: The court's decision on liability can be appealed prior to the determination of the issue of damages. Rule 505 authorizes an appeal of that decision, which was a final decision. 15. Questions of law and mixed law and fact In Altus Group Ltd. v. Calgary (Composite Assessment Review Board), 2011 ABQB 739, 528 A.R. 138, Justice Nation discussed the difference between a question of law and a question of mixed law and fact. Her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 20–21: 20 There has been considerable judicial analysis of exactly what is a question of law, as opposed to a question of mixed law and fact. This is because Courts of Appeal, as well as Courts involved in judicial review, and interpreting situations where there is a limited right to appeal, all have to battle with this distinction. Fruman, J.A. sets out the dilemma and importance of the distinction well in paras. 15 to 22 of Alberta (Worker's Compensation Board) v. Appeals Commission, 2005 ABCA 276. 21 Generally stated, an incorrect statement of the legal standard, or test, or an application of incorrect factors in applying the law to the facts is clearly an error of law. The law must not only be correctly stated, but that correct interpretation of the law must be applied to the facts, when engaged in applying the law to the facts. Where there is a discretion involved in applying the law to the facts, the application of the discretion is not a question of law, but a question of mixed law and fact. However, if a wrong legal principle is used in the application of the law to the facts, or in the exercise of the discretion, there is an error of law. 16. Liability to Pay Solicitor's Account A decision about the liability to pay a solicitor's account falls outside R. 505(3) (now 14.5). The narrow issue to be decided on this application is whether the Chambers judge's decision that Joel Hector was personally liable for the account for legal services provided by MacKimmie Matthews is a decision as to “costs only”. It is common ground that the definition of costs under the Alberta Rules of Court includes the account of a solicitor to his client… The Alberta Rules of Court, as a whole, are designed to facilitate the expedient administration of justice by regulating court procedure. Rule 505(3) exists to bring finality, to litigation and to conserve the appellate court's time by screening appeals on issues of costs alone. The Alberta Rules of Court provide a summary procedure for the taxation of costs before a taxing officer who has some expertise in the area of settling costs, both party and party costs and solicitor client costs. The taxation officer's orders are subject to an appeal to the Court of Queen's Bench. There is no other appeal without the leave of the Court of Queen's Bench. The taxation officer has a broad discretion in settling costs. The taxation officer is limited to questions relating to a quantum alone and cannot resolve other issues which may arise between the parties. If another issue arises, as it did in this case, the taxation officer refers the question to the court for resolution. Similarly, the award by a trial or Chambers judge of party and party costs is a discretionary order which may only be appealed with leave of the Court of Queen's Bench. Because of the discretionary nature of the order, the order should be and is only subject to appeal in limited circumstances, with leave and not as of right. (See rule 609 …). However, a ruling by a Chambers judge respecting liability for a solicitor's account requires the trial of an issue of fact as [to] the identity of the party who retained the solicitor and agreed either expressly or impliedly to pay the solicitor's fees. A ruling on this issue of fact impacts not only on the issue of the payment of the solicitor's account, but also establishes the nature of the contractual relationship between the parties for other purposes, for instance, issues dealing with solicitor client confidentiality, solicitor's liability, etc. That is not a discretionary order nor is the ruling one which relates to “costs alone”. Pursuant to [rule] 505(1), such a ruling may be appealed without leave. MacKimmie Matthews v. Hector (1998), 219 A.R. 163 (C.A.), at 164-65, per McFadyen J.A.

sentences.text: Commentary § 14.4:1 Rule 14.4 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Right to Appeal is Statutory In Québec (Communauté urbaine) v.
Services de santé du Québec, [1992] 1 S.C.R.
426, the Supreme Court of Canada stated that the right to appeal is a right created by statute.
At pp.

431–32 and 435, Madam Justice L'Heureux-Dubé, speaking for the court, said: The majority of the Court of Appeal rejected this argument as well, as in its opinion: … The right of appeal is a substantive right, an exceptional right which (except for a question of excess of jurisdiction by the Supreme Court, which is not the case here, Goodman v.
Rompkey et al., [1982] 1 S.C.R.
589), exists only if specifically created by legislation and only to the extent provided therein (Welch v.
412 at 428) … … as the majority of the Court of Appeal pointed out, the right of appeal is a statutory creation, the very existence of which is subject to precise rules … 2.
Appealing Interim Orders In Anand v.
Anand, 2016 ABCA 23, the Court had before it an appeal of an interim spousal support order made by Queen's Bench justice sitting in Chambers.
The Court made these comments about appeals of interim orders: 66 Interim spousal support orders have inherent frailties; the evidentiary record is inevitably incomplete.

Here, the viva voce special chambers judge had no ability to consider the interplay between spousal support and the division of matrimonial property, which future division may allow the respondent to generate income from assets.

67 This Court has repeatedly urged that parties not waste finite time and money appealing interim orders—time and money better spent achieving an equitable settlement, or getting a final determination at trial of all matters in issue: Hartley v Del Pero, 2010 ABCA 182 at para 27, 487 AR 248
Zaboschuk v Zaboschuk, 2012 ABCA 172 at para 5, [2012] A.J.
No.
575 (QL); Davies v Davies, 2015 ABCA 17 at para 6, [2015] A.J.
No.
35 (QL); FJN at para 6.
Moot Appeals An appeal is moot whether or not it suggests general questions of law or jurisdiction which could affect nonparties.
Given the laws of precedent, most appeals suggest such questions.

There are some exceptions to the general rule against deciding moot appeals. … Indeed, there are so many recent reported cases in Canada applying those exceptions, that one might gain the impression that the exception is the rule, and that appeals will rarely be dismissed as moot.
That is not the law.
There are real dangers in hearing moot appeals, quite apart from the obvious waste of court resources.
One danger is that a proceeding could go more or less by default, even by collusion, because a respondent would have little motive to fight it.
That is not likely here.
But sometimes the respondent may have a view or interest somewhat different from many or most people, leading him to be unaware of certain arguments.
Once the substantive issue has been settled, counsel may not recognize relevant authorities as relevant. … Another danger is that relevant arguments will not be put before the appeal court.
That could occur for the same reason.
But there are other reasons that the arguments might be incomplete.
One is that there can be no remedies in a moot suit, so issues must be split and only abstract ones be decided.

Another reason is that counsel thinking in the abstract without a specific factual problem will not imagine practical difficulties. … An abstract discussion of the law is likely to produce a vague judgment, difficult to apply in practice with any certainty.
Some government References to Canadian appellate courts in the past have illustrated that.
Anyone who asks a vague question is likely to get a vague answer.
A third danger is that the court may be led to enunciate a rule of law which hangs together in theory or logic, but is simply impractical.
Law exists for living human beings, but groups of human beings do not always act logically and consistently.
Sometimes it takes an actual dispute, or several, and experience, to show what will work and what will not.
A fourth danger is that the court hearing a moot appeal will enunciate too wide a rule of law.
Sometimes it is better to build the law a piece at a time, by trial and error, proceeding from one specific dispute to another.
Sometimes one must do that, because the topic is otherwise too complex, difficult, or unforeseeable.
A fifth danger is that the court will proceed with an inadequate evidentiary record.
That is particularly apposite here, where the appeal books seem to contain no evidence at all, except maybe a short report by an investigating officer employed by the Board.
If the union local led any evidence before the Board, it was not transcribed.
No one filed any affidavit in Queen's Bench.
Even if any facts were asserted to the Board in any of the written arguments, they have not been sworn to, nor been open to cross-examination.
Sometimes a respondent may have a smaller war chest than the appellant, or less motivation to spend large sums.
That too can lead to a lopsided record in a moot suit.
A sixth danger is that the moot appeal dragoons the respondent into acting as a sort of private Attorney General, or devil's advocate.
He or she must spend time and money on a question in which he or she has no present interests at risk.
That is unfair to him or her.
It may be useful to the appellant, or even to society, to clarify or build case law.
But why should the respondent have to finance that?
He or she is not the Legislature, nor even the Law Reform Institute.
This may be akin to forcing a litigant to buy law books and donate them to the courthouse library. …Wiebe v.
Labour Relations Board (Alta.) (2001), 281 A.R.
362 (C.A.) at 364-365, per curiam.

Application to Open Judgment Is Not an Appeal Actually, the application to open up my judgment is not, by its very nature, an appeal; rather it is an invitation to review a decision properly made at the time, but one which seeks variance because of the defendant's contention that the evidence which he provided me at the time (by affidavit) was erroneous.
The matter of weighing his former evidence with his fresh evidence would seem to be the exercising of the function of a court of original jurisdiction rather than that of a Court of Appeal.
National Arts Services Corp. v.
Bank of British Columbia (1981), 16 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 111 (Q.B.), at 115, per Cormack J.
When Appeal Lies to Court of Appeal … the appeal to this court only lies from an otherwise unimpeachable, unappealable, order of the Court of Queen's Bench.
C & A Electric Industries Ltd. v.
Gitersos (1983), 43 A.R.
C & A Electric Industries Ltd. was applied in Opi Ltd. v.
Harway Industrial Enterprises Ltd.
L.R.
If the appeal is as of right, no conditions on that right can be imposed.
According to Rule 505, because there is no statutory provision or Rule to the contrary, the appellant is entitled to appeal the order to this Court without leave.
Since leave is not required, no conditions on the right of appeal could be prescribed by this panel.
Horner v.
Adams (1996), 44 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 223 (C.A.), at 224, per curiam.
Who May Appeal In Marcaronies Hair Club and Laser Center Inc v.

Bank of Montreal, 2021 ABCA 40, 2021 CarswellAlta 235, the Court discussed who could bring an appeal pursuant to Rule 14.4: [37] It is correct that Rule 14.4(1) provides for an appeal to this Court from a decision of the Queen's Bench.
But notably, the Rule does not say who may appeal.
That is to be determined by this Court based on the applicable legislation and the Court's jurisdiction under the Judicature Act.
Rule 14.4(1) also includes the caveat “except as otherwise provided”, clearly implying therefore that any such claimed right to appeal under the Rules may be curtailed by other provisions.

This is reinforced by Rule 1.9 which provides that an enactment prevails over the Rules to the extent of any inconsistency. … … 41] As noted, this Court has recognized that there may be exceptional circumstances in which it would be appropriate to grant permission to appeal: Brewer
Société des Acadiens v Association of Parents, 1986 CanLII 66 (SCC), [1986] 1 SCR 549 at 594 [Société des Acadiens].

The Legislature has conferred broad authority on this Court under s 3 of the Judicature Act to entertain appeals from any decision of the Court of Queen's Bench. … [42] The test for whether a non-party should be granted permission to appeal centers on whether they would have been a proper party to the action.
That involves considering a number of factors, including whether their interests were represented at the proceeding: Société des Acadiens at 594. … 7.
Only Formal Judgment Can Be Appealed In Elizabeth Metis Settlement v.
Metis Settlements General Council (2004), 346 A.R.
86 (C.A.), orders were granted by a Chambers judge.
The decisions set out in the orders were not appealed, but the appellant did take issue with comments made by the learned Chambers judge in her reasons for decision.
The Court of Appeal held that one could not appeal the reasons in the absence of an appeal of the decision.
At p.
87, Berger J.A. said: … The Appellant acknowledges that it takes issue only with certain comments made by the presiding justice in chambers in her reasons for decision.
We do not view the impugned comments of the trial judge as declaratory in nature.
Only the formal disposition of a court can properly be the subject of appellate review.
The reasons, in a given case, may arguably taint the resulting order, in which case if the order is appealed, appellate intervention may be warranted.
But where no appeal is taken from the order pronounced in the court below, the appellate court is without jurisdiction to intervene. … In Kennedy v.

Trustees for the 1985 Sawridge Trust, 2017 ABCA 439, 2017 CarswellAlta 2698, the Court said: 8 Rule 14.8(1), which measures the time in which an appeal must be filed from the date of “pronouncement”, does not expand the scope of a permissible appeal to cover everything “pronounced” in the reasons for decision.
Appeals are only available from a “judgment, order or decision”, not the reasons.
Comments by the trial judge that do not form a part of his adjudication, and accordingly do not find their way into the formal order, cannot support an appeal.
In CCS Corporation v.
Secure Energy Service, 2018 ABCA 120, 2018 CarswellAlta 573, 68 Alta.
L.R.

575, “the appellant sought an order or declaration that certain findings of fact made by the case management judge do not apply to the Secure Respondents.” The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal “on jurisdictional grounds” and said: 13 We conclude this court has no jurisdiction to hear the appeal on the merits.
14 An appeal is from a decision, not from the reasons: Rayani v Yule & Company (Hong Kong) Limited, 1996 ABCA 35 at para 13
Elizabeth Metis Settlement v Metis Settlement General Council, 2004 ABCA 39 at para 1
SemCanada Crude Company (Companies' Creditors Arrangement Act), 2009 ABCA 244 at para 7
R v Elliott, 2014 ABCA 431 at para 4; and Huartt v Specialized Property Evaluation Control Services Ltd, 2016 ABCA 142 at para 6.
15 As noted by this court in Elizabeth Metis Settlement at para 1, “Only the formal disposition of a court can properly be the subject of appellate review”.

16 Further, r 14.4(1) of the Rules of Court provides that: Except as otherwise provided, an appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from the whole or any part of a decision of a Court of Queen's Bench judge sitting in court or chambers, or the verdict or finding of a jury.

17 Rule 14.1(1)(f) goes on to define “decision” as “the whole or any part of the decision of the court, person or tribunal from which an appeal lies and includes a judgment, order, decision, verdict, direction, determination or award and, where the context requires, includes the verdict or finding of a jury.” 18 The appellant did not appeal the decision to dismiss all of the claims against Pembina, save one.
Rather, the appellant seeks a declaration that certain of the case management judge's findings do not bind it.
Such a declaration raises issues of res judicata and issue estoppel that should properly be decided by the trial judge.
In ServiceMaster of Canada Limited v.
Meyer, 2019 ABCA 130, 2019 CarswellAlta 2118, 92 Alta.
L.R.
73, Justice Wakeling said: [31] The Alberta Rules of Court[7] allow a party to appeal against features of an order or judgment.
In the absence of a statutory provision to the contrary, which does not exist here, a party cannot appeal against reasons.
This statement was quoted with approval in Kaufmann v.
Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2019 ABCA 272, 2019 CarswellAlta 1375 at paragraph 9.
In Castle Building Centres Group Ltd. v.
Alberta Drywall & Stucco Supply Inc., 2023 ABCA 298, the Court of Appeal, at paragraph 12, reiterated that “[a]n appeal is from the order granted, not the reasons for it.” 8.
Scope of Appellate Review The Court of Appeal for Alberta enjoys a broad jurisdiction.
The Judicature Act, R.S.A.
3, states: 3.
The Court of Appeal
(a) has all the jurisdiction and powers possessed by the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories en banc immediately before the Court's organization, and
(b) has jurisdiction and power, subject to the Rules of Court, to hear and determine
(i) all applications for new trials
(ii) all questions or issues of law
(iii) all questions or points in civil or criminal cases

(iv) all appeals or motions in the nature of appeals respecting a judgment, order or decision of (A) a judge of the Court of Queen's Bench, or (B) a judge of a court of inferior jurisdiction when an appeal is given by any other Act.

The provisions of the Judicature Act are supplemented by the Alberta Rules of Court, in particular rules 505 and 518 … These broad powers must, however, be read in light of the principles guiding appellate review as laid down by this court.

In particular it has been said on a number of occasions that where a trial judge makes a finding of fact based on the credibility of witnesses, an appeal court should not overturn that finding unless it can be shown that the finding was “palpably wrong”… The Alberta Court of Appeal has itself applied this restriction on a number of occasions.
In Colberg v.
Schumacher (1978), 12 A.R.
183 … Moir J.A. said at p.
190: In my respectful opinion the learned trial judge could have found that there was an acceptance of the appellant's offer by the respondent.
He did not do so.
Rather, he chose to accept the evidence given by the respondent in chief.
He heard the witness.
It was for the trial judge to decide if he accepted the whole of the respondent's evidence, part of it, or none of it.
Clearly he accepted the respondent's evidence in chief only.
The question is are we entitled to reverse that finding when there is evidence to support that finding?
As I read the authorities, particularly the Supreme Court of Canada in Stein v.
The Ship “Kathy K”, [1976] 2 S.C.R.
802, we can only do so if the learned trial judge was ‘palpably wrong’.
I do not think that he was, particularly in the light of the whole of the cross examination.
The learned trial judge had an advantage that we can never have.
He saw and heard the respondent give the evidence.
I am not prepared to say that he lost the advantage by making the finding he made.
Similar cautionary comments may be found in Carter v.
Ferguson, [1943] 2 W.W.R.
38 (Alta.
C.A.); Clarke v.
Gerbrandt (1984), 34 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 289 (C.A.), and Angus v.
Edmonton (1977), 3 A.R.

In the last two decisions the Court of Appeal did overturn the findings of a trial judge, but in Clarke on the ground that there was no evidence at all to support the finding and in Angus on the ground that the finding was based on expert evidence where credibility was not a factor.
Such circumstances constitute exceptions to the general rule requiring palpable and overriding error.
Molchan v.
Omega Oil & Gas Ltd.
L.R.
Although the above quote comes from the dissenting reasons of Wilson J., it can be taken as a correct statement of the law relating to the scope of appellate review.
Standards of Review In Al-Ghamdi v.
College and Association of Registered Nurses of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 81, 2020 CarswellAlta 369, 71 Admin.
L.R.

(6th) 40, the Court of Appeal set out the standards of review for a number of types of appeals: [6] The standard of review on questions of law is correctness, on questions of fact is palpable and overriding error, and on questions of mixed law and fact is palpable and overriding error unless there is an extricable error of law: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, paras 7–37, [2002] 2 SCR 235.
[7] The standard of review with respect to the finding of civil contempt varies with the issue.
Where the appeal involves a question of law, the standard of review is correctness.
Where the issue relates to the exercise of discretion, the standard is one of reasonableness.
Findings of fact and inferences of fact underlying a finding of contempt are reviewed for palpable and overriding error.

The finding of contempt in a particular case involves the application of a legal standard to the facts, meaning it is a mixed question of fact and law and is reviewable on the palpable and overriding error standard: Demb v Valhalla Group Ltd, 2015 ABCA 29, paras 25-26, 593 AR 368
RO v DF, 2016 ABCA 170, para 29, 36 Alta LR
(6th) 282; Lymer v Jonsson, 2018 ABCA 36, paras 18-19, leave denied [2018] SCCA No 193.

[8] The standard of review on whether a litigant is vexatious is discretionary and, absent an error of law, is reviewed for reasonableness: Liu v Matrikon Inc., 2010 ABCA 383, paras 10, 16–17, 493 AR 378
Thompson v International Union of Operating Engineers Local No 995, 2017 ABCA 193, para 23, [2017] AJ No 620.
[9] The standard of review with respect to the proper interpretation of rr 3.15, 3.28, 3.68 and 7.3 is correctness.

With respect to the application of those rules to findings of fact where the chambers judge has exercised discretion, the standard of review is reasonableness: McGowan v Lang, 2015 ABCA 217, para 21, 602 AR 168
O'Connor Associates Environmental Inc v MEC OP LLC, 2014 ABCA 140, para 12, [2014] 6 WWR 231.

[10] In striking a claim under r 3.68(2)(d) as disclosing no reasonable claim or for abuse of process the standard of review is correctness: Waquan v Canada (Attorney General), 2017 ABCA 279, para 16, [2018] 4 WWR 361
Vanmaele v Maryniak, 2018 ABCA 179, para 6, [2018] AJ No 601.

However, assessment of the facts, application of the law to the facts, and ultimate determination as to whether to strike a claim, is discretionary and subject to reasonableness: Grenon v Canada Revenue Agency, 2017 ABCA 96, para 4, 49 Alta LR
(6th) 228; Nammo v Canada (Justice and Attorney General), 2015 ABCA 389, para 7, 609 AR 189; O'Connor, paras 11 and 13.
[11] The standard of review on the exercise of judicial discretion to refuse permission to amend pleadings is reviewable on the standard of reasonableness: AB v CD, 2008 ABCA 51, paras 9-10, 291 DLR
(4th) 359; Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated v Canada (Attorney General), 2009 NUCA 2, para 23, 457 AR 320.

[12] With respect to the orders for summary judgment, such orders are discretionary and, absent an error of law, are reviewed for reasonableness: 776826 Alberta Ltd v Ostrowercha, 2015 ABCA 49, para 7, 593 AR 391
Warkentin v Klein, 2009 ABCA 223, para 6, 457 AR 73
Amack v Wishewan, 2015 ABCA 147, para 27, 602 AR 62.
In Al-Ghamdi v.
College of Physicians and Surgeons of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 71, 2020 CarswellAlta 285, 68 Admin.
L.R.
(6th) 290, 6 Alta.
L.R.

(7th) 42, the Court set out the following standards of review: [9] The standards of review on a statutory appeal from an administrative tribunal are the same as those on other appeals: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para.
Those standards of review can be summarized as follows: (a) conclusions on issues of law are reviewed for correctness: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33 at para.
That includes questions of statutory interpretation, including interpretation of the tribunal's “home statute”.
(b) findings of fact, including inferences drawn from the facts, are reviewed for palpable and overriding error: Housen at paras.
10, 23; H.L. v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 SCC 25 at para.
(c) findings on questions of mixed fact and law call for a “higher standard” of review, because “matters of mixed law and fact fall along a spectrum of particularity”: Housen at paras.

A deferential standard is appropriate where the decision results more from a consideration of the evidence as a whole, but a correctness standard can be applied when the error arises from the statement of the legal test: Housen at paras.

(d) issues of fairness and natural justice are reviewed, having regard to the context, to see whether the appropriate level of “due process” or “fairness” required by the statute or the common law has been granted: Vavilov at para.

(e) the test on review for bias is whether a reasonable person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, and after having obtained the necessary information and thinking things through, would have a reasonable apprehension of bias.
In Schneider v.

Homenick, 2024 ABCA 344, additional reasons 2025 ABCA 39, the Court said: [14] The standard of review on questions of law is correctness, on questions of fact is palpable and overriding error, and on questions of mixed law and fact is palpable and overriding error unless there is an extricable error of law: Housen v Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33, paras 7-37, [2002] 2 SCR 235
R v Le, 2019 SCC 34, para 23, [2019] 2 SCR 692
R v Ledesma, 2021 ABCA 143, para 32, 403 CCC
(3d) 268, leave to appeal to SCC denied, 2022 CanLII 26226.

[15] Palpable and overriding error is a highly deferential standard. “Palpable” means that an error is obvious. “Overriding” means an error that goes to the very core of the outcome of a case: Benhaim v St-Germain, 2016 SCC 48, paras 38, 39, [2016] 2 SCR 352
R v Kruk, 2024 SCC 7, paras 97, 98, 433 CCC
Appeals Involving the Rules of Court In Courtoreille v.
Edmonton (City), 2008 ABCA 90, 2008 CarswellAlta 273, 429 A.R.
58, the Court discussed the appropriate standard of review.
At paragraph 6, the Court said: 6 The standard of review was recently stated in Phillips v.
Cowan, [2007] A.J.
No.
319, 2007 ABCA 101 at para.
4: The proper interpretation of the Rules of Court is a matter of law and reviewable on a correctness standard.
The application of a the rule to a set of facts is a question of mixed fact and law and subject to the standard of palpable and overriding error. … In Golden Estate v.
Neilson, 2011 ABCA 338, 2011 CarswellAlta 2281, 519 A.R.
L.R.
165, the Court said, at paragraphs 12-13: 12 An interpretation of the Rules of Court is reviewable on a standard of correctness.

However, orders relating to the nature and scope of questioning (formerly, examinations for discovery) are within a chambers judge's discretion and are entitled to considerable deference: Tremco Incorporated v Gienow Building Products Ltd, 2000 ABCA 105, 255 AR 273 and Devon Canada Corporation v PE-Pittsfield LLC, 2008 ABCA 393, 446 AR 62.

13 The standard of review is therefore that found in Trout Lake Store Inc v Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 2003 ABCA 259 at para 17, 330 AR 379: The proper interpretation of the Rules is a matter of law which is reviewable on the standard of correctness.
The application of the Rules to a set of facts is a matter of mixed fact and law and subject to the standard of palpable and overriding error.

Appeals from Discretionary Orders … the standard of review for the exercise of the discretion whether to grant summary judgment, or strike a claim, or to permit a matter to go to trial, is whether an error of law has been made or the decision is unreasonable in that no weight or insufficient weight has been given to relevant considerations.
See Russell Food Equipment (Calgary) Ltd. v.
Valleyfield Investments Ltd.
Blomme v.
Herman (1993), 145 A.R.
16 (C.A.), at 17-18, per the court.
In Prefontaine v.
Veale (2003), 24 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 223 (C.A.), the Court said, at p.
229: Initial appellate review occurs in two stages.
First, the appellate court, applying a standard of correctness, considers whether an error of law has been made: Housen v.
Nikolaisen, [2002] 2 S.C.R.
If no error of law was made, the first appellate court next considers whether the decision arrived at was reasonable.
The standard of review at this stage, absent an extricable error in principle, is palpable and overriding error: Housen v.
Nikolaisen at p.
And Lieberman J.A. said: … this court will not normally interfere with the discretion exercised by a chambers judge but is entitled to do so in certain circumstances.
Those circumstances are, to a great extent, outlined by Lord Diplock in Birkett v.
James, [1977] 2 All E.R.
801 (H.L.), where that learned law lord said at p.

804: Where leave is granted, an appellate court ought not to substitute its own ‘discretion’ for that of the judge merely because its members would themselves have regarded the balance as tipped against the way in which he had decided the matter.
They should regard their function as primarily a reviewing function and should reverse his decision only in cases either

(1) where they are satisfied that the judge has erred in principle by giving weight to something which he ought not to have taken into account or by failing to give weight to something which he ought to take into account
Demarco Oil & Gas Inc. v.
309506 Alberta Ltd.
Case Management Orders—Standard of Review In Ashraf v.
SNC Lavalin ATP Inc., 2017 ABCA 95, 2017 CarswellAlta 462, the Court said: 4 The first two decisions being contested are case management decisions.
This Court has made clear that such decisions are entitled to considerable deference.
In Goodswimmer v Canada (Attorney General), 2015 ABCA 253, 606 AR 291, the Court stated at para 8: Case management judges are owed deference.
Absent an error of law, this Court will not interfere with a chambers judge's exercise of discretion unless the result was unreasonable.
This is particularly so when many competing factors must be balanced: Mikisew Cree First Nation v Canada, 2004 ABCA 279 at para 10 (2004), 354 AR 279.
5 The third decision goes further and deals with the merits of the summary judgment application.

The standard of review for the case management judge's conclusions on this subject was described in Dingwall v Dornan, 2014 ABCA 89, 572 AR 106 at para 19: Absent an error of law, the standard of review on an appeal of a summary judgment is reasonableness, given the discretionary nature of the remedy.
Questions of law are reviewed for correctness.

Errors of mixed fact and law, and errors of fact alone are reviewed on the standard of palpable and overriding error, unless the error of mixed fact and law involves an error relating to an extricable principle of law, in which case the standard is one of correctness: Condominium Corp No 0321365 v 970365 Alberta Ltd, 2012 ABCA 26 at paras 39 and 40, 519 AR 322, see also Hryniak v Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7 at para 84.
Order Transcript of Chambers Judge's Reasons It is imperative that counsel who are appealing a chambers order obtain a transcript of the chambers judge's reasons.
The Court of Appeal has invoked R.
599.1 to award non-recoverable costs against both appellant and respondent when they failed to order the transcript in a timely fashion (see annotation under R.
In Gunderson v.
Jenkins (1998), 216 A.R.
344 (C.A.), the court said, at p.
345: We are all of the view that the appellant should have his costs of this appeal, with the exception of any costs in connection with the appeal book.
We are specifically excluding costs connected to the appeal book because, although the reasons of the chambers judge were recorded, they were not transcribed and included in the appeal book.
It has taken some considerable effort on our part to obtain them from counsel.
The bar cannot continue to ignore the fact that reasons are ususally recorded in chambers in the Court of Queen's Bench, at least in special chambers.
They can then be transcribed, and they should be transcribed and included in the appeal book.
It is important that we have the reasons of the chambers judge before us when we consider an appeal.
Appeal of Liability Trial Before Damage Trial Heard In Jen-Col Construction Ltd. v.
Parkland (County) No.
352 (Q.B.), an order had previously been granted permitting the severance of liability and damages into two separate trials.
The issue then became whether the decision in the liability trial could be appealed before the trial on damages was held.
In holding that it could, Veit, J., at p.
354, said: The court's decision on liability can be appealed prior to the determination of the issue of damages.
Rule 505 authorizes an appeal of that decision, which was a final decision.
Questions of law and mixed law and fact In Altus Group Ltd. v.
Calgary (Composite Assessment Review Board), 2011 ABQB 739, 528 A.R.
138, Justice Nation discussed the difference between a question of law and a question of mixed law and fact.
Her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 20–21: 20 There has been considerable judicial analysis of exactly what is a question of law, as opposed to a question of mixed law and fact.
This is because Courts of Appeal, as well as Courts involved in judicial review, and interpreting situations where there is a limited right to appeal, all have to battle with this distinction.
Fruman, J.A. sets out the dilemma and importance of the distinction well in paras.
15 to 22 of Alberta (Worker's Compensation Board) v.
Appeals Commission, 2005 ABCA 276.
21 Generally stated, an incorrect statement of the legal standard, or test, or an application of incorrect factors in applying the law to the facts is clearly an error of law.
The law must not only be correctly stated, but that correct interpretation of the law must be applied to the facts, when engaged in applying the law to the facts.
Where there is a discretion involved in applying the law to the facts, the application of the discretion is not a question of law, but a question of mixed law and fact.
However, if a wrong legal principle is used in the application of the law to the facts, or in the exercise of the discretion, there is an error of law.
Liability to Pay Solicitor's Account A decision about the liability to pay a solicitor's account falls outside R.

The narrow issue to be decided on this application is whether the Chambers judge's decision that Joel Hector was personally liable for the account for legal services provided by MacKimmie Matthews is a decision as to “costs only”.

It is common ground that the definition of costs under the Alberta Rules of Court includes the account of a solicitor to his client… The Alberta Rules of Court, as a whole, are designed to facilitate the expedient administration of justice by regulating court procedure.
Rule 505(3) exists to bring finality, to litigation and to conserve the appellate court's time by screening appeals on issues of costs alone.

The Alberta Rules of Court provide a summary procedure for the taxation of costs before a taxing officer who has some expertise in the area of settling costs, both party and party costs and solicitor client costs.
The taxation officer's orders are subject to an appeal to the Court of Queen's Bench.
There is no other appeal without the leave of the Court of Queen's Bench.
The taxation officer has a broad discretion in settling costs.
The taxation officer is limited to questions relating to a quantum alone and cannot resolve other issues which may arise between the parties.
If another issue arises, as it did in this case, the taxation officer refers the question to the court for resolution.
Similarly, the award by a trial or Chambers judge of party and party costs is a discretionary order which may only be appealed with leave of the Court of Queen's Bench.
Because of the discretionary nature of the order, the order should be and is only subject to appeal in limited circumstances, with leave and not as of right.
(See rule 609 …).

However, a ruling by a Chambers judge respecting liability for a solicitor's account requires the trial of an issue of fact as [to] the identity of the party who retained the solicitor and agreed either expressly or impliedly to pay the solicitor's fees.

A ruling on this issue of fact impacts not only on the issue of the payment of the solicitor's account, but also establishes the nature of the contractual relationship between the parties for other purposes, for instance, issues dealing with solicitor client confidentiality, solicitor's liability, etc.
That is not a discretionary order nor is the ruling one which relates to “costs alone”.
Pursuant to [rule] 505(1), such a ruling may be appealed without leave.
MacKimmie Matthews v.
Hector (1998), 219 A.R.
163 (C.A.), at 164-65, per McFadyen J.A.

paragraphs.text: (1) Except as provided in this rule, no appeal is allowed to the Court of Appeal from the following types of decisions unless permission to appeal has been obtained: (a) a decision of a single appeal judge; (b) any pre-trial decision respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits; (c) any ruling during trial, where the appeal is brought before the trial is concluded; (d) a decision made on the consent of the parties; (e) a decision as to a costs award only, but an appeal or cross appeal is not “as to a costs award only” if a related substantive decision is also being appealed; (f) any decision where permission to appeal is required by an enactment; (g) any decision in a matter where the controversy in the appeal can be estimated in money and does not exceed the sum of $25000 exclusive of costs; (h) any decision on security for costs; (i) any decision of the Court of King's Bench sitting as an appeal court under rule rule 10.26, 10.44 or 12.71; (j) any appeal by a person who has been declared a vexatious litigant in the court appealed from. (2) Permission to appeal decisions of single appeal judges under subrule (1)(a) must be sought from the same judge who made the decision that is to be appealed. (3) No appeal is allowed under subrule (1)(a) from a decision of a single appeal judge granting or denying permission to appeal. (4) No appeal is allowed under subrule (1)(j) from an order denying the vexatious litigant permission to institute or continue proceedings. Alta.
