paragraphs.text: Commentary § 14.5:1 Rule 14.5 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 14.5. 1. Generally In PWM Loss Prevention Services Inc. v. Lay, 2014 ABCA 376, 2014 CarswellAlta 2093, the employer (PWM Loss Prevention) sought judicial review in the Court of Queen's Bench of an order of the Director of Employment and Immigration Standards Program. The application for judicial review was dismissed. The employer applied for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal [the amount at issue was $2,564.42; consequently permission was required under R. 14.5(1)(g)]. Mr. Justice McDonald reviewed the law relating to an application for permission to appeal the decision of a reviewing judge. His Lordship said, at paragraphs 10–13: 10 A chambers judge must, on an application such as this, be satisfied that there is a reasonable prospect of success on the appeal itself in order to grant leave under Rule 14.5(1)(g). I cite in support of this proposition, the decision of this court in Correia v Koska, 2005 ABCA 184 (single judge). 11 In Jahelka v Alberta (Human Rights & Citizenship Commission), 2008 ABCA 82 Justice Wittmann of this court (as he then was) considered the factors that had been set out in Jeerh v Yorkton Securities Inc., (an earlier decision of this court cited at, 2005 ABCA 64 at para 21). 12 Justice Wittmann enumerated the factors to be as follows: • whether there is an arguable case (having regard to the standard of review on appeal); • whether there is a question of law or jurisdiction at issue; • whether the law or precedent is of importance to others or the public; • the practical effect on the parties and the result in the particular case; • whether there will be undue prejudice to a party; • whether there is a bar to the appeal (i.e. would the appeal be nugatory or moot); • whether the expense of a further appeal is commensurate with the value to be gained from the appeal; and • the standard of review on the appeal if leave was to be granted. 13 On an appeal from a decision of a reviewing judge, the appellate court must determine, as a matter of law, whether the reviewing judge adopted the correct standard of review and furthermore whether, as a matter of law, the reviewing judge properly applied that standard of review: Dr Q v College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, 2003 SCC 19 at para 43. In Saldiran v. Saldiran, 2022 ABCA 318, 2022 CarswellAlta 2620, Justice Feehan said: [8] Permission can be granted if the applicant establishes that there is: (a) a question of general importance to the community or of sufficient importance to the parties to justify the allocation of the public and private resources associated with an appeal; (b) a possible error of law; (c) an unreasonable exercise of discretion; or (d) a misapprehension of important facts: Settlement Lenders Inc v Blicharz, 2016 ABCA 109, para 1, leave to appeal refused, [2016] SCCA No 275. At least one of the substantial criteria should be made out or it is not in the public interest to review the single judge decision: Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403, para 11. [9] An important consideration is whether the applicant has identified a serious issue justifying another level of review. Assessment of the seriousness of the issue involves consideration of a number of factors: the perceived strength of the argument; the importance of the issue to the parties; and the general importance of the issue within the larger legal system. The applicant need not show a likelihood of success, but must demonstrate more than that the appeal is not frivolous. The Court must be satisfied that the issue has a reasonable chance of success. Merely wanting to reargue the same matters is not sufficient: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261, para 6, 58 Alta LR (6th) 109. In Xu v. Ma, 2024 ABCA 81, Justice Feth gave this overview of the law governing applications for leave to appeal a decision of a single appeal judge: [5] … This application comes before me pursuant to Rules 14.5(1)(a) and 14.5(2) and is heard in writing. My role under 14.5(1)(a) is that of gatekeeper. Permission to appeal a decision of a single judge of the Court of Appeal is to be granted rarely, and an applicant must show a “compelling reason to require the applicant and respondent to reargue and three judges of the Court of Appeal to decide an issue” (emphasis in original): Ouellette et al v Law Society of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 283 at paras 9, 14. This application for permission to appeal is not a rehearing of the applicant’s second application to restore the appeal. Rather, the “applicant must demonstrate a reviewable and material issue of law worthy of review by a full panel of the Court”: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261 at para 4, 58 Alta LR (6th) 109 [Alberta Health]. [6] That issue of law must arise from my order denying the applicant’s second restoration application, not the original trial decision. As set out in Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403 at para 10: The burden on an applicant to obtain permission to appeal an order of a single judge of this Court under Rule 14.5(2) is to establish that the order of the single judge being reviewed: (a) raises a question of general importance which on its own deserves panel review; (b) rests on a reviewable and material issue of law worthy of panel review; (c) involves an unreasonable exercise of discretion which had a meaningful effect on the outcome of the decision and the outcome is worthy of panel review or (d) rests on a palpable and overriding error of important facts affecting the order made and the order is worthy of panel review. Other factors that may be considered include “whether there are conflicting decisions on the point; the standard of review that would be applied on the appeal; and whether there are other good reasons why a full panel of the Court should review the order under appeal”: Alberta Health at para 5. 2. When is Rule 14.5(1) engaged? In Ozark Resources Ltd v. TERIC Power Ltd, 2020 ABCA 51, 2020 CarswellAlta 201, 49 C.P.C. (8th) 227, Justice Antonio said: [20] Permission of this court is required to commence an appeal from “any pre-trial decision respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits”: Rule 14.5(1)(b). … [22] The inclusion of an adjournment ruling in an order does not colour the entirety of the order. Whether an appeal triggers Rule 14.5(1) will depend on the relief requested on appeal: Wishewan v Amack, 2011 ABCA 386. That is, if the relief sought touches only on rulings for which permission is not required, then no permission is required. Where some of the relief sought is captured by Rule 14.5(1) and some is not, then permission is required to proceed with the former grounds while the latter may proceed as of right: Phillips v Avena, 2005 ABCA 138 at paras 5–7. In Alston v Foothills No. 31 (District of), 2021 ABCA 150, 2021 CarswellAlta 1032, Madam Justice Schutz said: [3] Rule 14.5 stipulates exceptions to the general rule [14.4(1)] that appeals lie to the Court of Appeal from the whole or any part of a decision of a Court of Queen's Bench judge sitting in court or chambers. The relevant sub-rule 14.5(1)(b), requires that permission to appeal be obtained if the appeal is from a decision of “any pre-trial decision respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits”. The respondent says this sub-rule is a complete bar to the applicants' appeal of the Order. I disagree. [4] First, sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) is not a complete bar merely because some paragraphs of the Order are pre-trial decisions respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits which on their own, would require permission to appeal. Put another way, if aspects of the appealed Order do not fit within sub-rule 14.5(1)(b)—or any other exception found in rule 14.5, permission to appeal is not required and there is no impediment to those paragraphs of the appealed Order proceeding. [5] Second, sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) only applies to a limited number of categories of procedural appeals. While rule 14.5(1)(b) may be interpreted broadly, it does not capture every pre-trial decision made by a Court of Queen's Bench judge that relates to litigation management; rather, the sub-rule provides this Court with a limited gate-keeping function in respect of certain appeals which do not determine all or some significant part of a party's substantive rights, and about which an appeal is often not a proportionate response: 1920341 Alberta Ltd v Jonsson, 2018 ABCA 231 at para 10. The general test for permission to appeal under rule 14.5 is that a) there is an important question of law or precedent, (b) there is a reasonable chance of success on appeal, and (c) the delay will not unduly hinder the progress of the action or cause undue prejudice: Platner v Platner, 2010 ABCA 342 at para 6. [6] I conclude sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) only requires the applicants to obtain permission to appeal paragraphs 4–8 of the Order. These paragraphs of the Order strictly relate to (a) an adjournment of the special chambers date previously set (paragraph 4), and (b) at paragraphs 5–8, provide time limits within which the parties would complete preparatory steps (filing affidavits; questioning on affidavits; exchanging briefs; scheduling the hearing), in advance of the substantive hearing of applicants' contempt application. 3. Rule 14.5(2)(a)—Test In Wolk v. Wolk, 2021 ABCA 301, 2021 CarswellAlta 2152, Justice Feehan said: [6] The law on permission to appeal a decision of a single judge to a panel of the Court of Appeal is thoroughly addressed in the recent decision Ouellette et al v Law Society of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 283. In that decision, Wakeling JA correctly stated that a decision of a single judge to allow an appeal to a panel of the Court of Appeal “will be rarely granted”, as it was “an extraordinary exercise of a single judge's authority”, para 9. [7] Wakeling JA said that such permission should be granted “only if there is a compelling reason to require the applicant and the respondent to reargue and three judges of the Court of the Appeal to decide an issue”: para 14 [emphasis in original]. See also Schulte, para 7; Wang, para 6, Hayden, para 13. [8] I do not take Wakeling JA to suggest that all of these factors must be addressed sequentially, nor are they determinative in every case. Hearing application for leave concurrently with hearing appeal? In Esfahani v. Samimi, 2021 ABCA 290, 2021 CarswellAlta 2059, Justice Slatter disagreed with a suggestion that there was a practice that the leave application in an arbitration appeal should be heard at the same time as the appeal is heard. His Lordship said: [1] In accordance with R. 14.5(1)(b), the applicant seeks permission to appeal a Family Docket Court Endorsement. That Endorsement directed that an application for permission to appeal an arbitration award would be adjourned over and heard together with the substantive appeal itself. … [9] The chambers judge implied that there is an established practice of hearing the application for permission to appeal concurrently with the appeal. There is no rule or practice direction authorizing that approach, and there are several recent decisions where the application for permission to appeal was heard as a preliminary matter: for example, K-Rite Construction Ltd v Enigma Ventures Inc., 2020 ABQB 566; TR Canada Inc v Cahill Industrial Ltd, 2021 ABQB 274 at para. 10; 719491 Alberta Inc v Canada Life Assurance Co, 2021 ABQB 226. There also does not appear to be another reported decision just like this in Alberta, that is a situation where a discrete application for permission to appeal was brought, and opposed, but that application was nevertheless deferred to be heard by the judge hearing the appeal. [10] There are cases where the application for permission to appeal and the appeal were apparently heard together, but no explanation is given of how that procedure was adopted: Dawson v Dawson, 2016 ABQB 167, 78 RFL (7th) 182; Pinder v Woodrow, 2015 ABQB 750, 71 RFL (7th) 380. [11] There are also some decisions where permission to appeal is refused, but the judge nevertheless expresses an opinion on the merits. It seems that all the issues were argued together, but again none of these cases explain how the combined procedure came to be adopted: for example, Heredity Homes (St Albert) Ltd v Scanga, 2009 ABQB 237, 471 AR 361, 18 Alta LR (5th) 271; Fuhr Estate; Warren v Alberta Lawyers' Public Protection Association (1997), 1997 CanLII 14925 (AB QB), 56 Alta LR (3d) 52, 208 AR 149. In some cases, it would appear that in the context in deciding whether permission to appeal should be granted, a discussion of the standard of review, the importance of the issue, or the strength of the applicant's case unfortunately evolved into an extensive consideration of the merits: see Athan Homes at para. 42; Central Alberta Rural Electrification Assn (Contract Policy Committee) v FortisAlberta Inc., 2012 ABQB 653 at para. 126, 71 Alta LR (5th) 170, 552 AR 11; Prairie Roadbuilders Ltd v Flatiron-Dragados-Aecon-Lafarge, 2019 ABQB 934, 1 CLR (5th) 45. [12] In addition, there are several decisions that involve an application for permission to appeal under s. 44(2) of the Arbitration Act, which requires permission to appeal, and an application to set aside the award under s. 45, which can be brought as of right and without permission. There is often overlap in the issues, and these reported decisions consider both whether permission to appeal should be granted and whether the award should be set aside: see Athan Homes Inc v Phan, 2021 ABQB 119; Allen v Renouf, 2020 ABQB 98, 36 RFL (8th) 199; Capital Power Corporation v Lehigh Hanson Materials Limited, 2013 ABQB 413, 565 A.R. 302; Clark v Unterschultz, 2020 ABQB 338, 41 RFL (8th) 28; Fuhr Estate v Husky Oil Marketing Company, 2010 ABQB 495, 35 Alta LR (5th) 83, 496 AR 232. These are not examples of the application for permission to appeal, and the appeal itself, being heard at the same time. [13] Where an application for permission to appeal under s. 44(2) is brought alongside an application to set aside the award under s. 45, one can understand why the parties might consent to hearing the two proceedings together. While the court is not bound by the consent of the parties on whether permission to appeal should be granted, the court might well acquiesce in the procedural choices made by the parties. It does not appear as if any objection was taken to the combined procedure in any of these reported cases. The court undoubtedly has a considerable procedural flexibility, but when a discrete application is brought for permission to appeal, and that application is opposed, the presumption is that the threshold issue of permission to appeal will be decided in advance. [14] It follows that the applicant has raised arguable issues in support of the proposed appeal, and there is no clear evidence of a practice in the Court of Queen's Bench supporting the approach taken in the Endorsement. 5. Part J of the former Court of Appeal Consolidated Practice Directions applied, inter alia, to appeals from orders that did not finally determine all or some significant part of the substantive rights and issues: s 2(a)(i) and (ii). In other words, it applied to certain procedural and interlocutory orders that virtually always amount to an exercise of discretion: Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd v National Oilwell Varco, Inc., 2010 ABCA 381 at para 5. Additionally, in those decisions, the issue in question may be rendered moot or can be appealed after a trial or other final decision has been rendered. As well, the standard of review for such discretionary orders is very high. Appeals in such cases are generally contrary to the policy adopted by this Court which discourages litigation by installments and appeals of preliminary issues where success is unlikely: Robertson v Wasylyshen (2003), 2003 ABCA 279 (Can LII), 339 A.R. 169 (C.A.). These factors are particularly acute for appeals which fall under Part J.3(a)(ii) and (iii) because those categories are most likely to be cases where an appeal is likely to cause a worse effect, namely, delay. For example, if a party appeals a timing order, a decision by this Court will inevitably take some months from filing the appeal. If that much delay has no practical effect on complying with the deadline set by the order under appeal, in most cases, no reasonable person would appeal. If the appeal has no practical effect, the appeal is likely academic or useless. Alternatively, if there is a practical effect on the action and no stay, the appeal will almost inevitably become moot. Alternatively, if there is a stay of a timing order, the appellant wins the appeal de facto even before the appeal is argued. Because of this situation, the mere arguability or importance of an issue is not a sufficient test. In addition, given the highly deferential standard of review, intervention by this Court is unlikely and the reluctance to permit such appeals is increased. Leave is intended to discourage appeals in those narrow cases, absent some reasonable chance of success. To further that objective, leave to appeal should be rare. A high threshold is required which takes into consideration the merit of the appeal and the importance as a precedent of law or practice weighed against the practical effect on the case which is being delayed. Judicial resources will be used more effectively in a case like this if leave is not required. Accordingly, the appeal from the ruling that no leave is required for a cross-appeal on costs alone in these circumstances is dismissed. In Brill v. Brill, 2017 ABCA 235, 2017 CarswellAlta 1246, Madam Justice Strekaf said, at paragraph 2: 2 Rule 14.5(1)(e) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 requires permission to appeal “a decision as to costs only”. Permission should be granted sparingly: Bun v Seng, 2015 ABCA 165 at para 4. The purpose of the predecessor of this rule was “to bring finality to cost orders and to conserve this Court's time by screening out hopeless appeals on the issue of costs alone”: Colborne Capital Corp v 542775 Alberta Ltd, 1996 ABCA 94 at para 10, 38 Alta LR (3d) 127. The same rationale underlies the current rule. In Bun v. Seng, 2015 ABCA 165, Justice Picard said: 4 Rule 14.5(1)(e) requires a party to obtain permission to appeal a decision as to costs only. The case law is clear that permission to appeal costs orders should be granted sparingly, and a party seeking permission to appeal such an award must meet a high threshold: Lameman v Alberta, 2011 ABQB 724 at para 9, 521 AR 121; Gutierrez v Jeske, 2005 ABQB 971 at para 4, 396 AR 1. This Court has held that it is appropriate to rely on the test for permission to appeal a costs award that was established under the former appellate Rules: Jackson v Canadian National Railway Company, 2015 ABCA 89 at para 10. That test requires an applicant to demonstrate: (i) a good arguable case having sufficient merit to warrant scrutiny by this Court; (ii) issues of importance to the parties and in general; (iii) that the costs appeal has practical utility; and (iv) no delay in proceedings caused by the costs appeal. In Rock River Developments Ltd. v. Village of Nampa, 2024 ABCA 42, Justice Ho noted that if the appeal as to costs relates to a matter involving less than $25,000, then “[u]nlike the Cairns factors”, the above “criteria are applied rigidly: if the applicant does not establish all criteria, the application must fail….” (paragraph 13). And the Alberta Court of Appeal said: A discretionary order as to costs only cannot be appealed without leave, notwithstanding an error of law or fact. C & I Insulation Distributors Ltd. v. 318648 Alberta Ltd. (1989), 98 A.R. 305 at 306 (C.A.). Consent Judgments: In Yakimyshyn v. Yakimyshyn (1994), 22 Alta. L.R. (3d) 305 (C.A.), Côté J.A. dealt with an application for a fiat to file a notice of motion seeking leave to appeal a consent judgment of the Court of Queen's Bench when that court had refused leave to appeal. His Lordship said, at p. 308: It will be noted that it [R. 505(3)] says “subject to any appeal”, which in my view means that without proper leave, the Court of Appeal cannot hear any kind of appeal relating to a consent judgment. That is so whether that appeal be directly from the judgment, or from a refusal of leave to appeal. In Alberta (Director, Parentage & Maintenance Act) v. C. (B.) (1993), 12 Alta. L.R. (3d) 422 (Q.B.), Deyell J., at pp. 425–26, said the following about “judicial discretion”: First, returning to Campbell & Co. v. Pollack, [[1927] A.C. 732] Viscount Cave at p. 811-12 describes “judicial discretion” in the context of deciding whether to grant an order as: This discretion, like any other discretion, must of course be exercised judicially, and the judge ought not to exercise it against the successful party except for some reason connected with the case. Thus, if—to put a hypothesis which in our Courts would never in fact be realized—a judge were to refuse to give a party his costs on the ground of some misconduct wholly unconnected with the cause of action or of some prejudice due to his race or religion or (to quote a familiar illustration) to the colour of his hair, then a Court of Appeal … although it may deem his reasons insufficient and may disagree with his conclusion, is prohibited by the statute from entertaining an appeal from it. Similarly, Lord Atkinson states at p. 814: But there is a settled practice of the Courts that in the absence of special circumstances a successful litigant should receive his costs, that it is necessary to show some ground for exercising a discretion by refusing an order which would give them to him. The discretion must be judicially exercised, and therefore there must be some grounds for its exercise, for a discretion exercised on no grounds cannot be judicial. Secondly, the more recent case of Currie v. Thomas (1985), 3 C.P.C. (2d) 42 (B.C. C.A.), provides a helpful description of “judicial discretion” in the context of a costs appeal. Esson J.A. makes the following observations in this regard at pp. 53–54: The discretion must, of course, be exercised judicially. That, at least, means that it is not an arbitrary power to be capriciously exercised. In Morrison v. Morrison, [1928] 2 D.L.R. 998 (Ont. C.A.), Middleton J.A. said at p. 179-80: Despite the warning of Lord Coleridge, C.J., in Huxley v. West London Extension Ry. Co. (1886), 17 Q.B.D. 373 at p. 376, that the discretion is not an arbitrary power but a judicial discretion to be “exercised on legal principles, not by chance medley, nor by caprice, nor in temper,”… Finally, Mr Justice Deyell noted at p. 428 of Alberta (Director, Parentage & Maintenance Act) v. C. (B.), that “… no leave to appeal lies for a refusal to grant an application for leave to appeal a costs order …” In R. v. Chisan (1994), 21 Alta. L.R. (3d) 95 (C.A.), the Alberta Court of Appeal considered whether a party who had been denied leave to appeal could then appeal that denial, At pp. 97–98, the court said: The question we must first ask is: Does this panel have the requisite jurisdiction to entertain an appeal from a decision to deny leave to appeal? In our view the answer is: No. This point was settled in Western Securities Ltd. v. Foothills (Municipal District), [1982] 1 W.W.R. 171, [17 Alta. L.R. (2d) 164] (Alta. C.A.). At p. 172, Kerans J.A. said: In my view, the governing rule is that a leave denial is final for all purposes. … Kerans J.A. reasoned that the rule laid down in [Ernewein v. Canada (Minister of Employment), [1980] 1 S.C.R. 639], namely that the Supreme Court of Canada should not interfere with a decision to deny leave made by a single justice of the Federal Court of Appeal, was analogous to and binding in a situation where an appeal was taken from the leave decision made by one member of the Court of Appeal: the panel should not interfere with the leave decision made by a single justice of he Court of Appeal. He stated at p. 173: Here, the legislature decided upon a policy whereby an intermediate appellate court, which is to say, a single judge of this court, is to decide whether or not an appeal will be permitted to proceed. This court, therefore, should respect this differentiation and recognize this legislative policy, and that should end the matter so far as any further appeal here is concerned. Also see, “Test to Be Applied in Granting Leave”, infra. 13. When a Non-party Is Involved In 358427 Alberta Inc. v. Monenco Advisory Services Ltd. (1999), 242 A.R. 1 (Q.B.), the defendant Monenco had been successful at trial but unsuccessful in obtaining an order of costs against an entity not a party to the action. The plaintiff then appealed the substantive trial decision, and the issue arose as to whether Monenco needed leave to appeal the dismissal of its costs application. Smith J. ruled that leave was not required, and, at pp. 2–3, said: One might argue leave ought to be required where the nonparty has been spared at the trial level and the main appeal involves only the parties. However, that argument rings hollow where the nonparty has been assessed costs of the trial. Clearly the same test should apply whether the nonparty has won or lost on the costs application in the trial court. In my view, there is no compelling reason to treat the cost result involving a nonparty any differently than one in which the parties are involved. Requiring leave, on the other hand, has the potential to render an injustice to the nonparty required to pay costs. Therefore, I declare, where, as here, there is an appeal of the main action, leave is not required to appeal a costs result involving a nonparty. 14. Scope of Respondent's Arguments if Unrestricted Leave Granted The general rule as to the scope of this Court's jurisdiction in hearing appeals seems clear. When an unrestricted leave to appeal is granted, a respondent may advance any argument which would support the judgment below. This is subject to the sole restriction that the argument would not have required additional evidence to be adduced at trial. Idziak v. Canada (Minister of Justice), [1992] 3 S.C.R. 631, at 643–44, per Cory J. 15. “Costs” Unlikely to include lawyers' fees In Tallcree First Nation v. Rath & Company, 2020 ABCA 433, 2020 CarswellAlta 2301, the law firm had entered into a contingency agreement with its client. Under the terms of the agreement, an account was rendered. The client applied under Rule 10.13 for a review of the contingency agreement. The Review Officer was asked to determine whether the contingency fee was reasonable under Rule 10.9. The Review Officer held the fee was reasonable; the client appealed that decision to a chambers judge who revoked the Review Officer's decision. The law firm wanted to appeal the chambers judge's order, and sought “a declaration confirming that they have a right to appeal that decision because it is not a decision ‘as to costs only’, or, if it is a decision ‘as to costs only’, for permission to appeal.” On the question of whether the decision about the contingency fee was “as to costs only”, Madam Justice Khullar said: [14] It is doubtful that the decision under appeal is a decision “as to costs only”. It concerns a dispute about the recovery of lawyers' fees between a lawyer and his or her client, not the payment of costs between parties to litigation. The word “costs” in the Rules normally refers to costs payable between parties to a lawsuit and phrase “recoverable fees” refers to the fees due from a client to his or her lawyer: see Divisions 1 and 2, Part 10 of the Alberta Rules of Court. The definitions section of the Rules defines “costs award” as the amount payable by one party in a lawsuit to another party in accordance with r 10.31 (a court-ordered costs award) or r 10.43 (an assessment officer's certification of costs payable between parties). [15] It would be odd if the word “costs” in r 14.5(1)(e) has a different meaning than it has in other parts of the Rules. [16] I note that there are two single judge decisions under pre-2010 versions of the Rules which held that a decision as to “costs” alone, for the purposes of determining whether leave to appeal is needed, includes the review of a lawyer's recoverable fees against his or her client: Kohut v Wilson, 2002 ABCA 247 at para 6 and Matt, Owens, Stinchcombe, Sattin & Coultry v Neilson, 1980 ABCA 349 at para 9. The persuasive value of these decisions is limited, the former because it provides no reason for including a review of a lawyer's charges with the category of a “decision as to costs only” and the latter because it was based on the layout of the Supreme Court Rules of Alberta in force in 1980—in particular, that the rules dealing with costs between parties and review of lawyer-client fees were grouped together under Part 47. [17] Even if a Review Officer's review of a lawyer's charges to his or her client amounts to “a decision as to costs alone” for the purpose of r 14.5(1)(e), a review of a contingency fee agreement does not. The policy behind r 14.5(1)(e) is to screen out appeals of discretionary costs (or review) decisions which rarely raise questions of principle and would be reviewed on a deferential standard: Beazer v Tollestrup, 2019 ABCA 10 at paras 2-3. A review of lawyers' accounts is a largely discretionary exercise but a review of a contingency fee agreement for reasonableness raises issues of principle about whether (and when) clients who enter into such an agreement and allow the lawyer to fulfil the contingency can decline to pay the contractually-agreed contingency fee. [18] In short, the policy behind the rule requiring permission to appeal for “a decision as to costs alone” does not apply to an appeal of a review of a contingency fee agreement. No previous decision of this Court has held that such an appeal requires permission to appeal under r 14.5(1)(e) or its predecessors. [19] I am satisfied that permission to appeal is not needed, as the decision under appeal is not a decision “as to costs alone.” 16. Standard of Review in Appeals of Costs Awards In Wang v. Alberta, 2022 ABCA 79, 2022 CarswellAlta 627, leave to appeal refused 2023 CarswellAlta 60 (S.C.C.), the Court said: [16] A discretionary decision on costs may be set aside if an appellate court finds that a judge has misdirected herself on the applicable law or made a palpable error in her assessment of the facts: Deans v Thachuk, 2005 ABCA 368 at para 16. [17]“[R]eversing a lower court's discretionary decision is also appropriate where the lower court gives no or insufficient weight to relevant considerations”: Penner v Niagara (Regional Police Services Board), 2013 SCC 19 at para 27. 17. Rule 14.5(1)(e) In Starke Capital Corp. v. Strategic Acquisition Corp., 2017 ABCA 217, 2017 CarswellAlta 1181, Justice Strekaf discussed when leave to appeal a costs order is not required. At paragraphs 5–7, her Ladyship said: 5 The rationale underlying the predecessor of this rule, r 505(3), in the context of the cross-appeal on costs only, was explained in Colborne Capital Corp v 542775 Alberta Ltd (1996), 184 AR 63, 38 Alta LR (3d) 127 (CA) at para 11: The mere fact that a cross-appeal might raise different issues on the question of costs does not justify requiring the Respondent to seek leave of the Court of Queen's Bench. Having heard the main appeal, the cross-appeal on costs will take up relatively little of this Court's time. Judicial resources will be used more efficiently in a case like this if leave is not required. 6 The language in Rule 14.5(1)(e) directs that permission to appeal a cost award is not required “if a related substantive decision is also being appealed”. Although it is desirable, it is not necessary that the appeals on the substantive decision and the costs decision be heard at the same time. 7 This court has previously determined that permission is not required when the substantive decision and the costs decision were delivered at different times, even when the costs appeal and the appeal on the substantive decision will not be heard at the same time: Brown v Silvera, 2011 ABCA 88, 505 AR 168; Rensonnet v Uttl, 2016 ABCA 316. In Beazer v. Tollestrup, 2019 ABCA 101, 2019 CarswellAlta 490, Justice Hughes said: [2] Rule 14.5(1)(e) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 requires permission to appeal “a decision as to costs only”. Permission to appeal costs orders should be granted sparingly: Bun v Seng, 2015 ABCA 165 (CanLII) at para 4, [2015] AJ No 534. The purpose of the predecessor of this rule was “to bring finality to cost orders and to conserve this Court's time by screening out hopeless appeals on the issue of costs alone”: Colborne Capital Corporation v 542775 Alberta Ltd, 1996 ABCA 94 (CanLII) at para 10, 38 Alta LR (3d) 127. The same rationale underlies the current rule. In Cold Lake Industrial Park GP Ltd. v. Abt (Estate), 2022 ABCA 23, 2022 CarswellAlta 188, Madam Justice Ho said: [21] The test for permission to appeal a decision that relates to costs only was outlined in Brill v Brill, 2017 ABCA 235 at para 3: (i) the applicant must identify a good, arguable case having enough merit to warrant scrutiny by the court; (ii) the issues must be important, both to the parties and in general; (iii) the appeal must have some practical utility; and (iv) the court should consider the effect of delay in proceedings caused by the appeal. 18. The Rule Does Not Apply to Costs under the Expropriation Act In Thoreson v. Alberta (Minister of Infrastructure) (2007), 79 Alta. L.R. (4th) 75 (Alta. C.A.), the Court said, at p. 77: …Rule 505(3) applies to civil litigation costs, and not to expropriation costs ordered under section 39 of the Act. Section 39 ensures that an owner of expropriated property is indemnified for all reasonable costs actually incurred for the purpose of determining the compensation due from an expropriating authority. This is not limited to litigation costs. Costs of this kind are akin to damages and do not fall under Rule 505(3). 19. Test to Be Applied in Granting Leave to Appeal Costs Order In 1985 Sawridge Trust v. Kennedy, 2017 ABCA 368, 2017 CarswellAlta 2303, 61 Alta. L.R. (6th) 21, Justice Slatter made these comments about applications for leave to appeal a costs order (and, in particular, costs awards against lawyers personally under R. 10.50): 1 F.F. SLATTER J.A.:—The applicant, who was counsel for one of the parties in this litigation, seeks leave to appeal the decision reported as 1985 Sawridge Trust v Alberta (Public Trustee), 2017 ABQB 530. That decision found the applicant personally liable for the costs of the proceedings on a solicitor and own client basis. 2 The general rule in Alberta is that any party is entitled to one level of appeal as a matter of right. In some exceptional cases, an appeal is only allowed with permission, including an appeal of any decision “as to costs only”: R. 14.5(1)(e). This rule is primarily intended to screen out potential appeals involving details of a costs award that do not justify a further level of review. It also reflects the fact that awards of costs are highly discretionary, and subject to a deferential standard of review. 3 The test for permission to appeal a costs award includes whether the applicant can show: (1) a good arguable case having sufficient merit to warrant scrutiny by a full panel of this Court; (2) issues of importance to the parties and in general; (3) the costs appeal has practical utility; and (4) no delay in proceedings will be caused by the costs appeal: Bun v Seng, 2015 ABCA 165 at para. 4 and Jackson v Canadian National Railway, 2015 ABCA 89 at paras. 9-10, 599 AR 237. 4 The Rules of Court contain a number of presumptions about costs awards. For example, R. 10.29 creates a presumption that the successful party is entitled to costs, and a presumption that costs are awarded on a “pay as you go” basis, not just at the end of the litigation. Schedule C creates a presumptive scale of costs. Costs that are consistent with the presumptions, guidelines and rules set out in the Rules of Court are resistant to appellate review, making appeals inappropriate. That is one reason that permission is required to appeal a decision as to costs only, and explains the outcome in cases like Brill v Brill, 2017 ABCA 235, which is easily distinguishable from the present situation. Further, appeals on the details of costs awards (e.g., which Column applies, was second counsel required, etc.) are rarely appropriate. 5 However, where a costs award raises more general issues, or issues of principle, or large sums are involved, a further appeal may well be justified. One example is Condominium Corp. No. 9813678 v Statesman Corp., 2011 ABQB 489, 52 Alta LR (5th) 252 which concerned whether a Bullock order could include double costs generated by an offer to settle. Another is Young v Young, [1990] BCJ No 1051, [1990] BCWLD 1239, which considered the liability of non-parties for costs, and which eventually resulted in the leading decision Young v Young, [1993] 4 SCR 3 at para. 253. A person subjected to an out-of-the-ordinary costs award will often have a legitimate basis for appealing, and where there is doubt permission to appeal should be granted. 6 Costs awards against lawyers personally are recognized by R. 10.50 as being available as a form of sanction:

sentences.text: Commentary § 14.5:1 Rule 14.5 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Generally In PWM Loss Prevention Services Inc. v.

Lay, 2014 ABCA 376, 2014 CarswellAlta 2093, the employer (PWM Loss Prevention) sought judicial review in the Court of Queen's Bench of an order of the Director of Employment and Immigration Standards Program.
The application for judicial review was dismissed.
The employer applied for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal [the amount at issue was $2,564.42; consequently permission was required under R.
Mr.
Justice McDonald reviewed the law relating to an application for permission to appeal the decision of a reviewing judge.

His Lordship said, at paragraphs 10–13: 10 A chambers judge must, on an application such as this, be satisfied that there is a reasonable prospect of success on the appeal itself in order to grant leave under Rule 14.5(1)(g).
I cite in support of this proposition, the decision of this court in Correia v Koska, 2005 ABCA 184 (single judge).

11 In Jahelka v Alberta (Human Rights & Citizenship Commission), 2008 ABCA 82 Justice Wittmann of this court (as he then was) considered the factors that had been set out in Jeerh v Yorkton Securities Inc., (an earlier decision of this court cited at, 2005 ABCA 64 at para 21).

12 Justice Wittmann enumerated the factors to be as follows: • whether there is an arguable case (having regard to the standard of review on appeal); • whether there is a question of law or jurisdiction at issue; • whether the law or precedent is of importance to others or the public; • the practical effect on the parties and the result in the particular case; • whether there will be undue prejudice to a party; • whether there is a bar to the appeal (i.e. would the appeal be nugatory or moot); • whether the expense of a further appeal is commensurate with the value to be gained from the appeal; and • the standard of review on the appeal if leave was to be granted.

13 On an appeal from a decision of a reviewing judge, the appellate court must determine, as a matter of law, whether the reviewing judge adopted the correct standard of review and furthermore whether, as a matter of law, the reviewing judge properly applied that standard of review: Dr Q v College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia, 2003 SCC 19 at para 43.
In Saldiran v.
Saldiran, 2022 ABCA 318, 2022 CarswellAlta 2620, Justice Feehan said: [8] Permission can be granted if the applicant establishes that there is:
(a) a question of general importance to the community or of sufficient importance to the parties to justify the allocation of the public and private resources associated with an appeal
(b) a possible error of law
(c) an unreasonable exercise of discretion; or
(d) a misapprehension of important facts: Settlement Lenders Inc v Blicharz, 2016 ABCA 109, para 1, leave to appeal refused, [2016] SCCA No 275.
At least one of the substantial criteria should be made out or it is not in the public interest to review the single judge decision: Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403, para 11.
[9] An important consideration is whether the applicant has identified a serious issue justifying another level of review.

Assessment of the seriousness of the issue involves consideration of a number of factors: the perceived strength of the argument; the importance of the issue to the parties; and the general importance of the issue within the larger legal system.
The applicant need not show a likelihood of success, but must demonstrate more than that the appeal is not frivolous.
The Court must be satisfied that the issue has a reasonable chance of success.
Merely wanting to reargue the same matters is not sufficient: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261, para 6, 58 Alta LR (6th) 109.
In Xu v.

Ma, 2024 ABCA 81, Justice Feth gave this overview of the law governing applications for leave to appeal a decision of a single appeal judge: [5] … This application comes before me pursuant to Rules 14.5(1)(a) and 14.5(2) and is heard in writing.
My role under 14.5(1)(a) is that of gatekeeper.

Permission to appeal a decision of a single judge of the Court of Appeal is to be granted rarely, and an applicant must show a “compelling reason to require the applicant and respondent to reargue and three judges of the Court of Appeal to decide an issue” (emphasis in original): Ouellette et al v Law Society of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 283 at paras 9, 14.
This application for permission to appeal is not a rehearing of the applicant’s second application to restore the appeal.

Rather, the “applicant must demonstrate a reviewable and material issue of law worthy of review by a full panel of the Court”: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261 at para 4, 58 Alta LR (6th) 109 [Alberta Health].
[6] That issue of law must arise from my order denying the applicant’s second restoration application, not the original trial decision.

As set out in Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403 at para 10: The burden on an applicant to obtain permission to appeal an order of a single judge of this Court under Rule 14.5(2) is to establish that the order of the single judge being reviewed:
(a) raises a question of general importance which on its own deserves panel review
(b) rests on a reviewable and material issue of law worthy of panel review
(c) involves an unreasonable exercise of discretion which had a meaningful effect on the outcome of the decision and the outcome is worthy of panel review or
(d) rests on a palpable and overriding error of important facts affecting the order made and the order is worthy of panel review.

Other factors that may be considered include “whether there are conflicting decisions on the point; the standard of review that would be applied on the appeal; and whether there are other good reasons why a full panel of the Court should review the order under appeal”: Alberta Health at para 5.
When is Rule 14.5(1) engaged?
In Ozark Resources Ltd v.
TERIC Power Ltd, 2020 ABCA 51, 2020 CarswellAlta 201, 49 C.P.C.

(8th) 227, Justice Antonio said: [20] Permission of this court is required to commence an appeal from “any pre-trial decision respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits”: Rule 14.5(1)(b). … [22] The inclusion of an adjournment ruling in an order does not colour the entirety of the order.
Whether an appeal triggers Rule 14.5(1) will depend on the relief requested on appeal: Wishewan v Amack, 2011 ABCA 386.
That is, if the relief sought touches only on rulings for which permission is not required, then no permission is required.

Where some of the relief sought is captured by Rule 14.5(1) and some is not, then permission is required to proceed with the former grounds while the latter may proceed as of right: Phillips v Avena, 2005 ABCA 138 at paras 5–7.
In Alston v Foothills No.

31 (District of), 2021 ABCA 150, 2021 CarswellAlta 1032, Madam Justice Schutz said: [3] Rule 14.5 stipulates exceptions to the general rule [14.4(1)] that appeals lie to the Court of Appeal from the whole or any part of a decision of a Court of Queen's Bench judge sitting in court or chambers.
The relevant sub-rule 14.5(1)(b), requires that permission to appeal be obtained if the appeal is from a decision of “any pre-trial decision respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits”.
The respondent says this sub-rule is a complete bar to the applicants' appeal of the Order.
I disagree.

[4] First, sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) is not a complete bar merely because some paragraphs of the Order are pre-trial decisions respecting adjournments, time periods or time limits which on their own, would require permission to appeal.

Put another way, if aspects of the appealed Order do not fit within sub-rule 14.5(1)(b)—or any other exception found in rule 14.5, permission to appeal is not required and there is no impediment to those paragraphs of the appealed Order proceeding.
[5] Second, sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) only applies to a limited number of categories of procedural appeals.

While rule 14.5(1)(b) may be interpreted broadly, it does not capture every pre-trial decision made by a Court of Queen's Bench judge that relates to litigation management; rather, the sub-rule provides this Court with a limited gate-keeping function in respect of certain appeals which do not determine all or some significant part of a party's substantive rights, and about which an appeal is often not a proportionate response: 1920341 Alberta Ltd v Jonsson, 2018 ABCA 231 at para 10.
The general test for permission to appeal under rule 14.5 is that a) there is an important question of law or precedent
(b) there is a reasonable chance of success on appeal, and
(c) the delay will not unduly hinder the progress of the action or cause undue prejudice: Platner v Platner, 2010 ABCA 342 at para 6.
[6] I conclude sub-rule 14.5(1)(b) only requires the applicants to obtain permission to appeal paragraphs 4–8 of the Order.
These paragraphs of the Order strictly relate to
(a) an adjournment of the special chambers date previously set (paragraph 4), and

(b) at paragraphs 5–8, provide time limits within which the parties would complete preparatory steps (filing affidavits; questioning on affidavits; exchanging briefs; scheduling the hearing), in advance of the substantive hearing of applicants' contempt application.
Rule 14.5(2)(a)—Test In Wolk v.

Wolk, 2021 ABCA 301, 2021 CarswellAlta 2152, Justice Feehan said: [6] The law on permission to appeal a decision of a single judge to a panel of the Court of Appeal is thoroughly addressed in the recent decision Ouellette et al v Law Society of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 283.

In that decision, Wakeling JA correctly stated that a decision of a single judge to allow an appeal to a panel of the Court of Appeal “will be rarely granted”, as it was “an extraordinary exercise of a single judge's authority”, para 9.

[7] Wakeling JA said that such permission should be granted “only if there is a compelling reason to require the applicant and the respondent to reargue and three judges of the Court of the Appeal to decide an issue”: para 14 [emphasis in original].

He said that compelling reason exists only if the following criteria are met: 1. the issue is of general importance to the community or of sufficient importance to the parties to justify the allocation of private resources … and public resources … associated with an appeal: para 15, nn 23–24
See also Vysek v Nova Gas International Ltd, 2002 ABCA 112, para 34, [2002] 10 WWR 70, 82
Carbone v Whidden, 2015 ABCA 177, para 30
Schulte v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 268, para 7
Settlement Lenders Inc v Blicharz, 2016 ABCA 109, para 1, leave to appeal ref'd, [2016] SCCA No 275
Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403, para 10
Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261, para 6, 58 Alta LR
(6th) 109; Hayden v Hayden, 2020 ABCA 37, para 13; PricewaterhouseCoopers Inc v Perpetual Energy Inc., 2020 ABCA 254, para 6.
2. the issue presents a legal question the answer to which will be of precedential value in the area of the law engaged: para 16, n 25
See also Boychuk v Edmonton (Police Service), 2014 ABCA 163, para 37, [2014] 8 WWR 250
Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2015 ABCA 257, para 2, 78 CPC

3. the decision is the product of a misunderstanding of the law or a misapprehension of the evidence or both and these conditions substantially contributed to the decision the applicant seeks permission to appeal: para 18, n 27
See also Settlement Lenders, para 1
Al-Ghamdi, para 10
Wang, para 5
Perpetual Energy, para 6.
4. the proposed appeal has a reasonable chance of success: para 19, n 28.
See also Schulte, para 7; Wang, para 6, Hayden, para 13.
[8] I do not take Wakeling JA to suggest that all of these factors must be addressed sequentially, nor are they determinative in every case.
All of these factors are weighed holistically to determine whether overall it is in the interests of justice to allow an appeal to the panel.
Hearing application for leave concurrently with hearing appeal?
In Esfahani v.

Samimi, 2021 ABCA 290, 2021 CarswellAlta 2059, Justice Slatter disagreed with a suggestion that there was a practice that the leave application in an arbitration appeal should be heard at the same time as the appeal is heard.
His Lordship said: [1] In accordance with R.
14.5(1)(b), the applicant seeks permission to appeal a Family Docket Court Endorsement.

That Endorsement directed that an application for permission to appeal an arbitration award would be adjourned over and heard together with the substantive appeal itself. … [9] The chambers judge implied that there is an established practice of hearing the application for permission to appeal concurrently with the appeal.

There is no rule or practice direction authorizing that approach, and there are several recent decisions where the application for permission to appeal was heard as a preliminary matter: for example, K-Rite Construction Ltd v Enigma Ventures Inc., 2020 ABQB 566
TR Canada Inc v Cahill Industrial Ltd, 2021 ABQB 274 at para.
10; 719491 Alberta Inc v Canada Life Assurance Co, 2021 ABQB 226.

1 (Q.B.), the defendant Monenco had been successful at trial but unsuccessful in obtaining an order of costs against an entity not a party to the action.

Smith J. ruled that leave was not required, and, at pp.

However, that argument rings hollow where the nonparty has been assessed costs of the trial.
Clearly the same test should apply whether the nonparty has won or lost on the costs application in the trial court.
In my view, there is no compelling reason to treat the cost result involving a nonparty any differently than one in which the parties are involved.
Requiring leave, on the other hand, has the potential to render an injustice to the nonparty required to pay costs.
Therefore, I declare, where, as here, there is an appeal of the main action, leave is not required to appeal a costs result involving a nonparty.

15. “Costs” Unlikely to include lawyers' fees In Tallcree First Nation v.
Rath & Company, 2020 ABCA 433, 2020 CarswellAlta 2301, the law firm had entered into a contingency agreement with its client.
Under the terms of the agreement, an account was rendered.
The client applied under Rule 10.13 for a review of the contingency agreement.
The Review Officer was asked to determine whether the contingency fee was reasonable under Rule 10.9.
The Review Officer held the fee was reasonable; the client appealed that decision to a chambers judge who revoked the Review Officer's decision.

The law firm wanted to appeal the chambers judge's order, and sought “a declaration confirming that they have a right to appeal that decision because it is not a decision ‘as to costs only’, or, if it is a decision ‘as to costs only’, for permission to appeal.” On the question of whether the decision about the contingency fee was “as to costs only”, Madam Justice Khullar said: [14] It is doubtful that the decision under appeal is a decision “as to costs only”.
It concerns a dispute about the recovery of lawyers' fees between a lawyer and his or her client, not the payment of costs between parties to litigation.

The word “costs” in the Rules normally refers to costs payable between parties to a lawsuit and phrase “recoverable fees” refers to the fees due from a client to his or her lawyer: see Divisions 1 and 2, Part 10 of the Alberta Rules of Court.

The definitions section of the Rules defines “costs award” as the amount payable by one party in a lawsuit to another party in accordance with r 10.31 (a court-ordered costs award) or r 10.43 (an assessment officer's certification of costs payable between parties).
[15] It would be odd if the word “costs” in r 14.5(1)(e) has a different meaning than it has in other parts of the Rules.

[16] I note that there are two single judge decisions under pre-2010 versions of the Rules which held that a decision as to “costs” alone, for the purposes of determining whether leave to appeal is needed, includes the review of a lawyer's recoverable fees against his or her client: Kohut v Wilson, 2002 ABCA 247 at para 6 and Matt, Owens, Stinchcombe, Sattin & Coultry v Neilson, 1980 ABCA 349 at para 9.

The persuasive value of these decisions is limited, the former because it provides no reason for including a review of a lawyer's charges with the category of a “decision as to costs only” and the latter because it was based on the layout of the Supreme Court Rules of Alberta in force in 1980—in particular, that the rules dealing with costs between parties and review of lawyer-client fees were grouped together under Part 47.

[17] Even if a Review Officer's review of a lawyer's charges to his or her client amounts to “a decision as to costs alone” for the purpose of r 14.5(1)(e), a review of a contingency fee agreement does not.

The policy behind r 14.5(1)(e) is to screen out appeals of discretionary costs (or review) decisions which rarely raise questions of principle and would be reviewed on a deferential standard: Beazer v Tollestrup, 2019 ABCA 10 at paras 2-3.

A review of lawyers' accounts is a largely discretionary exercise but a review of a contingency fee agreement for reasonableness raises issues of principle about whether (and when) clients who enter into such an agreement and allow the lawyer to fulfil the contingency can decline to pay the contractually-agreed contingency fee.
[18] In short, the policy behind the rule requiring permission to appeal for “a decision as to costs alone” does not apply to an appeal of a review of a contingency fee agreement.
No previous decision of this Court has held that such an appeal requires permission to appeal under r 14.5(1)(e) or its predecessors.
[19] I am satisfied that permission to appeal is not needed, as the decision under appeal is not a decision “as to costs alone.” 16.
